Requirements — schemars-to-reflection-plugin-pipeline\\n\\n## Context\\n\\nEvery plugin in `op-dbus` is the single source of truth for its own contract. That contract begins with typed Rust structs, flows through `PluginSchema` (the published interface object), is registered on D-Bus at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`, serialized into `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`, compiled by `build.rs` into gRPC proto services, and exposed through `tonic-reflection` so any client can discover methods without a `.proto` file.\\n\\nThe pipeline works end-to-end today for method inputs. The gaps are:\\n- **State-field schemas** for most plugins are still hand-rolled with `simple_schema()` / `any_field()` instead of derived from typed structs via `schemars`.\\n- **Method input schemas** in `build.rs` generate `google.protobuf.Struct` I/O, not field-typed proto messages. Only the runtime-frozen `PerMethodGrpcServices` descriptor has real field types.\\n- **`method_decl_from_schemars`** is marked `#[deprecated]` — callers should use the `_with_output` variant everywhere.\\n- The canonical pattern (illustrated by `unix_socket.rs`) is not yet documented or enforced per-plugin.\\n\\nThis spec defines the requirements for completing and hardening the pipeline so schemars is the seed for every plugin's full contract and `PluginSchema` remains the sole published source of truth.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Functional Requirements\\n\\n### REQ-1 — The Plugin Is the Schema\\n\\n**REQ-1.1** Every plugin MUST own its schema function (`<plugin>_schema() -> PluginSchema`) co-located in its own file. Schemas MUST NOT be defined inline in any other module.\\n\\n**REQ-1.2** The re-export aggregator `plugin_schema_defs.rs` MUST remain a thin re-export-only module. No schema logic belongs there. Utility helpers (`method_decl_from_schemars_with_output`, `AckOutput`, `materialize_state_from_schema`, etc.) may remain as shared tooling.\\n\\n**REQ-1.3** `PluginSchema` remains the single published contract object. Schemars is the derivation tool, not a replacement for `PluginSchema`. The `schema()` method on `StatePlugin` always returns a `PluginSchema`, never raw schemars output.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-2 — State Structs Must Derive `JsonSchema`\\n\\n**REQ-2.1** Every plugin's primary state struct (the one whose fields become `PluginSchema.fields`) MUST derive `schemars::JsonSchema`. It MUST also derive `serde::Serialize` and `serde::Deserialize`.\\n\\n**REQ-2.2** Nested structs referenced from a state struct (e.g., `SocketEndpoint` inside `UnixSocketState`) MUST also derive `schemars::JsonSchema`.\\n\\n**REQ-2.3** The schema function MUST call `schemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json(name, version, description, &serde_json::to_value(schemars::schema_for!(StateStruct)).unwrap())` to produce `PluginSchema.fields`. Manual `FieldSchema` construction for state fields is forbidden for new and migrated plugins.\\n\\n**REQ-2.4** Where the struct's `Default` impl carries meaningful values, `apply_state_defaults(&mut schema, &simd_json::serde::to_owned_value(StateStruct::default()))` MUST be called after `plugin_schema_from_json` to propagate defaults into the schema.\\n\\n**REQ-2.5** The schemars-derived schema MUST be guarded by a test using `schemars_adapter::schema_diffs()` that proves the derived schema matches the previous hand-rolled reference (or, for new plugins, the intended contract). This test must be co-located in the plugin file.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-3 — OSCAL Subids Must Be Carried by the Struct\\n\\n**REQ-3.1** Every schema-level subid (the schema's own OSCAL identifier) MUST be declared on the state struct via `#[schemars(extend(\\\"x-oscal-subid\\\" = \\\"sch.<type>.<subject>.describe@vN\\\"))]`.\\n\\n**REQ-3.2** Every field-level subid MUST be declared on the struct field via `#[schemars(extend(\\\"x-oscal-subid\\\" = \\\"<category>.<type>.<subject>.<verb>@vN\\\"))]`.\\n\\n**REQ-3.3** `schemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json` already reads `x-oscal-subid` from the schemars JSON output and populates `PluginSchema.subids`. No post-hoc `schema.subids.insert(...)` is needed for fields that carry the annotation on the struct.\\n\\n**REQ-3.4** Subids that refer to method-level artifacts (e.g., `createunixsocket`) and have no corresponding struct field MAY be inserted into `schema.subids` imperatively after schema construction. This is the only acceptable use of imperative `subids.insert`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-4 — Method Declarations Must Be Typed\\n\\n**REQ-4.1** Every `MethodDecl` MUST be constructed via `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<Input, Output>(...)`. The deprecated `method_decl_from_schemars::<Input>()` variant MUST NOT be used in new or migrated code.\\n\\n**REQ-4.2** Every method input type MUST be a dedicated named struct (e.g., `SetDeviceInput`) deriving `schemars::JsonSchema`, `serde::Serialize`, `serde::Deserialize`. Anonymous `json!({...})` as `args` is forbidden for plugins that have typed structs.\\n\\n**REQ-4.3** Every method output type MUST be a named struct. For methods that return only success/failure, `AckOutput` from `plugin_schema_defs` MUST be used. For methods with richer return data, a dedicated `<Method>Output` struct deriving `schemars::JsonSchema` MUST be defined.\\n\\n**REQ-4.4** `MethodDecl.returns` MUST always be `Some(...)`. A `None` returns value is a contract gap. Callers that only need to know whether the call succeeded MUST return `AckOutput`.\\n\\n**REQ-4.5** Every `MethodDecl` MUST carry a valid OSCAL subid per the taxonomy in AGENTS.md § 4a. The subid uniqueness CI gate (`all_plugin_subids_are_valid_and_unique` in `default_registry.rs`) must pass.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-5 — `PluginSchema.methods` Drives `build.rs` Proto Generation\\n\\n**REQ-5.1** `build.rs` in `op-grpc-bridge` MUST continue to instantiate all plugins at compile time, read `PluginSchema.methods`, and generate `plugin_methods.proto` and `plugin_method_routes.rs`.\\n\\n**REQ-5.2** The generated `plugin_methods.proto` currently uses `google.protobuf.Struct` for all I/O. This is acceptable at the build-time level because the runtime `PerMethodGrpcServices` freezes proper typed descriptors. The two layers are complementary: build-time routes provide type-checked Rust trait dispatch; runtime descriptors provide typed reflection for clients. Both MUST remain in sync with `PluginSchema.methods`.\\n\\n**REQ-5.3** `build.rs` MUST emit `cargo:rerun-if-changed=../op-plugins/src/state_plugins` so that adding or modifying a plugin's method declarations triggers a rebuild. This is already present and MUST be preserved.\\n\\n**REQ-5.4** If a plugin's method set is empty, `build.rs` MUST silently skip it (no empty proto service). This is already the behavior and MUST be preserved.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-6 — `PerMethodGrpcServices` Produces Typed gRPC Reflection Descriptors\\n\\n**REQ-6.1** `PerMethodGrpcServices::create_frozen_services()` MUST produce `FileDescriptorProto` entries with field-typed input/output messages (not `google.protobuf.Struct`), derived from `MethodDecl.args` and `MethodDecl.returns` JSON schemas.\\n\\n**REQ-6.2** `freeze_plugin_method_reflection()` on `OperationGrpcServer` MUST be called before `build_operation_routes()`. The combined descriptor snapshot passed to `tonic_reflection::server::Builder` must include both the static domain proto descriptors and all per-method typed descriptors.\\n\\n**REQ-6.3** `tonic-reflection` v1 and v1alpha endpoints MUST both be mounted and must agree on the same combined descriptor.\\n\\n**REQ-6.4** A `grpcurl -plaintext <addr> describe` on the running server MUST enumerate every plugin service for every plugin that has at least one `MethodDecl`. This is the acceptance criterion for reflection completeness.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-7 — D-Bus Object Export\\n\\n**REQ-7.1** Every registered plugin MUST be exported as a D-Bus object at the canonical path `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin_name>` (underscored, lowercase) by `PluginRegistry::register()`. This is already enforced.\\n\\n**REQ-7.2** The D-Bus object interface name MUST be `org.opdbus.v1.Plugin`. Methods on the object are dispatched through `PluginDbusHost` using `PluginSchema.methods` as the authority. D-Bus XML introspection is NOT used to derive method shapes — `PluginSchema` is the sole authority.\\n\\n**REQ-7.3** The D-Bus method dispatch path MUST read `PluginSchema.methods` for capability enforcement, input validation, and routing. It MUST NOT read from `simple_schema()`-style anonymous JSON objects.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-8 — `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` and Manifest\\n\\n**REQ-8.1** `SchemaEngine` MUST write the aggregated `PluginSchema` JSON (as produced by `PluginSchema::to_json_schema()`) for every registered plugin to `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` keyed by plugin name.\\n\\n**REQ-8.2** The live-schema file is the runtime canonical source for `grpc_server.rs` capability enforcement and for `UnixSocketPlugin::read_desired()`. It MUST remain the single runtime read-path; no second shm file per plugin.\\n\\n**REQ-8.3** Writes to `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` MUST NOT go through Btrfs I/O. tmpfs/ramfs is the correct mount.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-9 — No Bypasses\\n\\n**REQ-9.1** No plugin MAY read live state by spawning a subprocess (`Command::new(\\\"wg\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"ip\\\")`, etc.) in its schema or dispatch path. The D-Bus object owns plugin state.\\n\\n**REQ-9.2** No plugin MAY define its method contract via a hardcoded `json!({\\\"type\\\": \\\"object\\\", \\\"additionalProperties\\\": true})` in a `MethodDecl.args` field. All `args` must be derived from a typed struct.\\n\\n**REQ-9.3** Legacy `SqlitePluginCatalog` and JSON-RPC polling loops MUST NOT be introduced. The `SchemaCatalog` / `SchemaEngine` path is the only valid catalog path.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### REQ-10 — Migration Contract\\n\\n**REQ-10.1** Plugins fall into three migration tiers:\\n\\n| Tier | State | Action required |\\n|------|-------|-----------------|\\n| **A — Complete** | State struct derives `schemars::JsonSchema`; `schema()` calls `plugin_schema_from_json`…100995 tokens Requirements\\n2. Design\\n3. Technical spec\\n4. Tasks\\n\\nKeep each pass narrow. Ask Kiro to write only the current document, then move\\nto the next one after the previous output is acceptable.\\n\\n## Practical Setup\\n\\nBefore running Kiro:\\n\\n- make sure `kiro-cli` is installed and updated\\n- make sure `kiro-cli-term` is available in the terminal session\\n- run the dotfiles integration if Kiro asks for it\\n- prefer a separate comparison folder when you want to compare Kiro output with\\n  a manual draft\\n\\nUseful checks:\\n\\n```bash\\nkiro-cli --version\\nkiro-cli doctor -a\\nkiro-cli integrations status dotfiles\\n```\\n\\nIf the terminal integration is missing, start the wrapper in the same shell:\\n\\n```bash\\nkiro-cli-term -- kiro-cli doctor -a\\n```\\n\\n## Prompt Pattern\\n\\nStart with requirements, then continue in order:\\n\\n```text\\nCreate requirements for <feature>.\\nCreate design for the same feature.\\nCreate technical spec and task list for the same feature.\\n```\\n\\nFor comparison work, tell Kiro to write into a separate folder, for example:\\n\\n```text\\nCreate a new spec folder at .kiro/specs/<name>-kiro/ and write:\\nrequirements.md, design.md, spec.md, tasks.md, and .config.kiro.\\n```\\n\\n## Boundary Rules\\n\\nWhen writing specs for this repository:\\n\\n- plugin schema stays in the plugin\\n- projection layers may read plugin data, but do not redefine it\\n- zeroclaw must not duplicate schema already handled elsewhere\\n- btrfs subvolumes are for local install/cache/rollback state, not duplicate schema trees\\n- transport layers should be explicit about native socket vs HTTP/gRPC-Web paths\\n\\n## Comparing Outputs\\n\\nIf you want to compare Kiro with a manual draft:\\n\\n1. create the manual draft in one folder\\n2. generate the Kiro version in a second folder\\n3. compare requirements, design, spec, and tasks side by side\\n4. keep the version that is tighter and more implementation-ready\\n\\nThis repo’s preference is to let Kiro write the spec files and then use the\\nmanual draft only as a check, not as a competing authority.\\n\"},{\"kind\":\"text\",\"data\":\"User id: 1000\\ndrwxr-xr-x 1 1000 1000 16 Jul 03 13:19 write into a separate folder, for example:\\n\\n```text\\nCreate a new spec folder at .kiro/specs/<name>-kiro/ and write:\\nrequirements.md, design.md, spec.md, tasks.md, and .config.kiro.\\n```\\n\\n## Boundary Rules\\n\\nWhen writing specs for this repository:\\n\\n- plugin schema stays in the plugin\\n- projection layers may read plugin data, but do not redefine it\\n- zeroclaw must not duplicate schema already handled elsewhere\\n- btrfs subvolumes are for local install/cache/rollback state, not duplicate schema trees\\n- transport layers should be explicit about native socket vs HTTP/gRPC-Web paths\\n\\n## Comparing Outputs\\n\\nIf you want to compare Kiro with a manual draft:\\n\\n1. create the manual draft in one folder\\n2. generate the Kiro version in a second folder\\n3. compare requirements, design, spec, and tasks side by side\\n4. keep the version that is tighter and more implementation-ready\\n\\nThis repo’s preference is to let Kiro write the spec files and then use the\\nmanual draft only as a check, not as a competing authority.\\n\"},{\"Text\":\"User id: 1000\\ndrwxr-xr-x 1 1000 1000 16 Jul 03 13:19 topic: voyage-plugin-cognitive-mcp-boundaries.\\n\\nRepo: operation-dbus-proto. Architecture rule: THE PLUGIN IS THE SCHEMA — op-plugins/src/state_plugins/*.rs each own a schemars-derived PluginSchema, projected to a D-Bus object + gRPC blob (see crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/plugin_object_blob.rs and docs/schema-coupled-plugin-blob-reflection-whitepaper.md for the blob model, which you should read first).\\n\\nOnly look at these crates — do not touch or propose changes based on docs/, deploy/, or scripts/:\\n- crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/embedding_model.rs (just-built generic embedding-provider surface: provider/model_id/endpoint/dimensions/model_digest fields, embed/list_models/get_config/set_model/update_config methods, holds the relocated VoyageModel enum for the voyage-4 trio)\\n- crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/large_language_model.rs (the sibling generation-surface plugin this one was modeled on — the pattern to compare against)\\n- crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/cognitive_mcp.rs (an EXISTING state plugin whose doc comment claims to be 'the canonical schema (every gRPC method, every MCP tool, every request/response field)' for op-cognitive-mcp — but grep across the repo shows nothing in crates/op-cognitive-mcp actually reads cognitive_mcp_schema() or CognitiveMcpPlugin; it is only referenced inside op-plugins' own lib.rs/mod.rs/plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs re-exports)\\n- crates/op-cognitive-mcp/** entirely (src/voyage.rs = VoyageClient with its own bearer-auth + MongoDB-vs-public endpoint autodetection + model selection, independent of any plugin; src/bin/rag-ingest.rs = CLI that embeds repomix content into Qdrant via that VoyageClient; src/client_config.rs = has a rag/search MCP tool wrapper; src/notebooklm.rs, src/activity_filter.rs)\\n- crates/op-state-store/src/plugin_schema.rs (self-documented as an intentional LEGACY compatibility catalog, NOT a second schema authority — has its own builtin_plugin_schema() entries; note whether it has anything relevant to voyage/cognitive-mcp, but do not propose deleting it, that is a separate decision)\\n\\nVerified facts to start from (already confirmed in this session, do not re-derive):\\n- crates/op-cognitive-mcp/Cargo.toml already has  as a dependency. crates/op-plugins/Cargo.toml has NO dependency back on op-cognitive-mcp. So there is no crate-cycle obstacle to op-cognitive-mcp consuming op-plugins schemas/blobs at runtime — the dependency already points the right direction, it is simply unused today.\\n- Voyage bindings were just consolidated in op-plugins: ctl_plane_chatbot, knowledge (now deleted), memory_plugin, and notebooklm (op-plugins state plugin, NOT the op-cognitive-mcp crate file of the same name) all now delegate via an embedding_plugin field naming embedding_model. op-cognitive-mcp's own voyage.rs/rag-ingest.rs were NOT touched and still instantiate VoyageClient directly, independent of the plugin.\\n- grep '.methods.insert(' count per plugin file: notebooklm.rs=106, login1.rs=23, dnsresolver.rs=20, zeroclaw.rs=18, json_render.rs=15, cognitive_mcp.rs=15, ovsdb_bridge.rs=14, btrfs_plugin.rs=12. The notebooklm.rs=106 figure looks anomalously high versus every other plugin and may be a loop-generated artifact (e.g. one method per notebook) rather than 106 hand-declared distinct methods — verify by reading the file before treating it as 'the plugin with the most methods.'\\n- crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/knowledge_plugin.rs was JUST DELETED this session for being an unconsumed one-way state mirror with zero real consumers anywhere in the repo (confirmed via repo-wide grep before deletion). cognitive_mcp.rs may be the same disease — verify whether it is truly dead/unconsumed or whether something non-obvious does read it (check op-web, op-mcp, op-grpc-bridge, MCP tool registration paths, not just direct Rust references — also check if 'register_plugin_projection_tools' mentioned in its doc comment actually surfaces it as a live MCP tool anywhere real).\\n\\nOpen questions the spec must resolve, each with a concrete recommendation (not just options):\\n1. Should embedding_model be renamed/refocused to a concrete  plugin (dropping the provider-agnostic abstraction) and absorb VoyageClient's actual HTTP logic (bearer auth, MongoDB-vs-public endpoint autodetection, model selection) directly into the plugin, so the plugin IS the Voyage integration rather than a wrapper around a separate client living in a different crate? Or should embedding_model stay a generic surface with voyage.rs remaining the concrete provider implementation it delegates to?\\n2. What should 'op-cognitive-mcp is schema driven' concretely mean given the dependency already exists unused? Specifically: should rag-ingest.rs and the rag/search MCP tool in client_config.rs stop instantiating VoyageClient directly and instead dispatch embed calls through the plugin (voyage/embedding_model) via its D-Bus object or blob, with op-plugins remaining the sole owner of provider config/auth/model selection?\\n3. Is crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/cognitive_mcp.rs dead code (delete it like knowledge_plugin), or is it the correct integration seam that op-cognitive-mcp should be wired to consume (i.e., op-cognitive-mcp should start reading its own bind-address/health/tool-registration config FROM this plugin's D-Bus projection instead of running fully independently)? Recommend one, with evidence.\\n4. Given verified fact 3 above (notebooklm.rs=106 method count anomaly), determine which plugin genuinely has the most schema-declared methods and confirm/correct the premise that 'the [cognitive-mcp] plugin has the most methods of all plugins' — if that premise is false, say so plainly.\\n5. Draw the exact crate boundary line: what schema/config/auth/model-selection logic belongs in op-plugins (the voyage plugin) as the single source of truth, versus what legitimately stays in op-cognitive-mcp (MCP tool surface exposed to external clients, rag-ingest CLI orchestration, search-time query assembly) — and name every current overlap/duplicate that should be removed once the boundary is drawn.\\n\\nOutput requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md linked as this repo's other .kiro/specs/* do. Ground every claim in the actual current code you read — do not assume based on file/function names alone; open and read the files listed above before writing conclusions. Do not write any implementation code — this is a spec/design pass only, no crate executor and MCP tool surface), eliminating the three duplicate\\nembedding implementations that currently exist across those two crates, and wiring `op-cognitive-mcp`\\nto read its own runtime configuration from the D-Bus projection its plugin already owns.\\n\\n## Context and Verified Baseline\\n\\nThese requirements are grounded in code read during this spec session. Every claim below references\\na specific file and observation.\\n\\n### What already exists and is correct\\n\\n- `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/embedding_model.rs` — generic embedding surface: `provider`,\\n  `model_id`, `endpoint`, `dimensions`, `status`, `available_models`, `model_digest`. Carries\\n  `VoyageModel` enum (voyage-4-large / voyage-4 / voyage-4-lite, shared 1024-dim space).\\n  `voyage_key_present()` checks three env vars. `config_state()` reads provider config from env.\\n  `live_state()` queries Ollama or sets status=online for Voyage iff key present. Five schema methods:\\n  `embed`, `list_models`, `get_config`, `set_model`, `update_config`. Self-registered via\\n  `inventory::submit!`. Seeds `/dev/shm` at op-grpc-bridge startup via `seed_missing_plugin_projections`.\\n\\n- `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/cognitive_mcp.rs` — `CognitiveMcpPlugin` with `apply_state()`\\n  that writes s6 env-dir files (`COGNITIVE_MCP_BIND`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_GRPC_BIND`, `WG_INTERFACE`, etc.)\\n  and calls D-Bus reload. {"timestamp":"2026-07-05T05:56:10.929Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_KBMYyhBBcvLiUML0OYdrZw5W","output":"Chunk ID: da08c9\nWall time: 0.0001 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 5232\nOutput:\nsh: line 1: printf: --: invalid option\nprintf: usage: printf [-v var] format [arguments]\nsh: line 1: printf: --: invalid option\nprintf: usage: printf [-v var] format [arguments]\n# Design — schemars-to-reflection-plugin-pipeline\n\n## Architecture Question: Can Schemars Seed Every Plugin While `PluginSchema` Remains the Published Source of Truth?\n\n**Yes. The answer is yes, and this is the settled architecture.**\n\nSchemars is the **derivation tool**. `PluginSchema` is the **published contract object**. They occupy different layers:\n\n```\nRust struct (schemars::JsonSchema derive)\n        │\n        │  schemars::schema_for!()  →  JSON Schema 2020-12 document\n        │\n        ▼\nschemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json()\n        │\n        │  Walks JSON, resolves $defs/$ref, maps types, extracts\n        │  x-oscal-subid, x-immutable-paths, constraints\n        │\n        ▼\nPluginSchema { fields, methods, subids, ... }  ←── PUBLISHED SOURCE OF TRUTH\n        │\n        ├──► /dev/shm/live-schema.json   (runtime canonical read)\n        ├──► D-Bus object at /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>\n        ├──► build.rs  →  plugin_methods.proto  +  plugin_method_routes.rs\n        └──► PerMethodGrpcServices  →  FileDescriptorSet  →  tonic-reflection\n```\n\nThe struct cannot be queried directly by callers. The `PluginSchema` is what every consumer sees. Schemars disappears at the boundary of `plugin_schema_from_json`. This means:\n- Adding a field to the state struct automatically surfaces it in D-Bus, in the JSON contract, in the GUI, and in `live-schema.json`.\n- Removing a field from the struct removes it everywhere — no possibility of drift.\n- The struct is the documentation; doc comments become field `description` strings.\n\nThe migration path is plugin-by-plugin. Nothing breaks during migration. The `PluginSchema` interface contract is unchanged.\n\n# Requirements — schemars-to-reflection-plugin-pipeline\n\n## Context\n\nEvery plugin in `op-dbus` is the single source of truth for its own contract. That contract begins with typed Rust structs, flows through `PluginSchema` (the published interface object), is registered on D-Bus at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`, serialized into `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`, compiled by `build.rs` into gRPC proto services, and exposed through `tonic-reflection` so any client can discover methods without a `.proto` file.\n\nThe pipeline works end-to-end today for method inputs. The gaps are:\n- **State-field schemas** for most plugins are still hand-rolled with `simple_schema()` / `any_field()` instead of derived from typed structs via `schemars`.\n- **Method input schemas** in `build.rs` generate `google.protobuf.Struct` I/O, not field-typed proto messages. Only the runtime-frozen `PerMethodGrpcServices` descriptor has real field types.\n- **`method_decl_from_schemars`** is marked `#[deprecated]` — callers should use the `_with_output` variant everywhere.\n- The canonical pattern (illustrated by `unix_socket.rs`) is not yet documented or enforced per-plugin.\n\nThis spec defines the requirements for completing and hardening the pipeline so schemars is the seed for every plugin's full contract and `PluginSchema` remains the sole published source of truth.\n\n---\n\n## Functional Requirements\n\n### REQ-1 — The Plugin Is the Schema\n\n**REQ-1.1** Every plugin MUST own its schema function (`<plugin>_schema() -> PluginSchema`) co-located in its own file. Schemas MUST NOT be defined inline in any other module.\n\n**REQ-1.2** The re-export aggregator `plugin_schema_defs.rs` MUST remain a thin re-export-only module. No schema logic belongs there. Utility helpers (`method_decl_from_schemars_with_output`, `AckOutput`, `materialize_state_from_schema`, etc.) may remain as shared tooling.\n\n**REQ-1.3** `PluginSchema` remains the single published contract object. Schemars is the derivation tool, not a replacement for `PluginSchema`. The `schema()` method on `StatePlugin` always returns a `PluginSchema`, never raw schemars output.\n\n---\n\n### REQ-2 — State Structs Must Derive `JsonSchema`\n\n**REQ-2.1** Every plugin's primary state struct (the one whose fields become `PluginSchema.fields`) MUST derive `schemars::JsonSchema`. It MUST also derive `serde::Serialize` and `serde::Deserialize`.\n\n**REQ-2.2** Nested structs referenced from a state struct (e.g., `SocketEndpoint` inside `UnixSocketState`) MUST also derive `schemars::JsonSchema`.\n\n**REQ-2.3** The schema function MUST call `schemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json(name, version, description, &serde_json::to_value(schemars::schema_for!(StateStruct)).unwrap())` to produce `PluginSchema.fields`. Manual `FieldSchema` construction for state fields is forbidden for new and migrated plugins.\nsh: line 1: printf: --: invalid option\nprintf: usage: printf [-v var] format [arguments]\n# Spec — schemars-to-reflection-plugin-pipeline\n\n## Summary\n\nThis spec defines the complete plugin-owned pipeline from typed Rust structs through `PluginSchema` to D-Bus, `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`, `build.rs` gRPC proto generation, and `tonic-reflection` descriptor exposure.\n\nThe central question this spec answers: **Can `schemars` be the seed for every plugin while `PluginSchema` remains the published single source of truth?** Yes. Schemars is the derivation tool. `PluginSchema` is the published contract. The translation layer is `schemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json`. See [design.md](./design.md) for the full architecture answer and layer-by-layer breakdown.\n\n---\n\n## Linked Artifacts\n\n| Artifact | File |\n|---|---|\n| Requirements | [requirements.md](./requirements.md) |\n| Design | [design.md](./design.md) |\n| Tasks | [tasks.md](./tasks.md) |\n\n---\n\n## Pipeline Overview\n\n```\nPlugin file (<plugin>.rs)\n    │\n    ├── State struct (#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)])\n    │       │\n    │       └── schemars::schema_for!() → JSON Schema 2020-12\n    │               │\n    │               └── schemars_adapter::plugin_schema_from_json()\n    │                       │\n    │                       ▼\n    ├── Method input/output structs (#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)])\n    │       │\n    │       └── method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<In, Out>()\nsh: line 1: printf: --: invalid option\nprintf: usage: printf [-v var] format [arguments]\n# Tasks — schemars-to-reflection-plugin-pipeline\n\nEach task is self-contained, targets one layer of the pipeline, and ends with a `cargo check` / `cargo test` green gate. Complete tasks in order — later tasks build on earlier ones.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 0 — Infrastructure Hardening\n\n### Task 0.1 — Enforce `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output` Everywhere\n\n**Requirements**: REQ-4.1, REQ-4.4\n\n**Context**: `method_decl_from_schemars` is marked `#[deprecated]`. All call sites must migrate to `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<Input, Output>`.\n\n**Steps**:\n1. Run `grep -rn \"method_decl_from_schemars::<\" crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/` to enumerate all deprecated call sites.\n2. For each call site: identify whether the method has a meaningful return value or just success/failure.\n   - If just success/failure: replace with `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<XyzInput, AckOutput>`.\n   - If richer return: define a `<Method>Output` struct deriving `schemars::JsonSchema` and use it.\n3. Verify no `method_decl_from_schemars::<` calls remain: `grep -rn \"method_decl_from_schemars::<\" crates/ | grep -v \"method_decl_from_schemars_with_output\"`.\n4. Run `cargo check -p op-plugins`.\n5. Run `cargo test -p op-plugins -- all_plugin_subids_are_valid_and_unique`.\n\n**Acceptance**: Zero deprecated-function call sites. CI subid gate passes.\n\n---\n\n### Task 0.2 — Add `PluginSchemaBuilder::method` Convenience Method\n\n**Requirements**: REQ-4.1, REQ-5.2\n\n**Context**: Several plugins construct `schema.methods.insert(...)` imperatively. The Persona & Naming Conventions\\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \\\"Snowball\\\" session.\\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\\\"Law Firm\\\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \\\"The Sled\\\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \\\"The Shuttle\\\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \\\"The Snowball\\\" (appended session ledger), and \\\"The Strike/Etch\\\" (generating the hash).\\n\\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \\\"Reality\\\")\\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\\n\\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\\n\\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\\n\\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\\n\\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\\\"systemctl\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"ip\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"s6-svc\\\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\\n\\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\\n\\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\\n\\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\\n\\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\\n\\n| category | what it classifies |\\n|---|---|\\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\\n\\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\\n\\n**Rules:**\\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\\n\\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\\n\\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\\n\\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\\n\\n#### 5. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only.      bus_type: BusType,\n        ovsdb: Arc<OvsdbDbusClient>,\n        schema_engine: Option<Arc<MutationEngine>>,\n    ) -> std::result::Result<Self, MirrorError> {\n        let connection = match ovsdb,\n            schema_engine,\n            connection,\n            published_objects: DashMap::new(),\n            plugin_registry: Arc::new(DashMap::new()),\n            grpc_server: None,\n with_grpc_server(mut self, grpc_server: Arc<OperationGrpcServer>) -> Self {\n        self.grpc_server = Some(grpc_server);\n        self\n    }\n\n    /// Start the mirror service.\n    ///\n    /// Performs an initial full-tree publication and then enters an event-driven\n    /// loop to publish deltas from all data sources.\n    pub async fn start(self: Arc<Self>) -> std::result::Result<(), MirrorError> {\n        tracing::info!(\"Starting D-Bus mirror publication service...\");\n\n        // Register ObjectManager at the root to manage EVERYTHING.\n        let om = If you do use one, make it short Title Case (1-3 words), wrap it in **…**, and do not add a blank line.\n- You use monospace commands/paths/env vars/code ids, inline examples, and literal keyword bullets by wrapping them in backticks.\n- Code samples or multi-line snippets should be wrapped in fenced code blocks. Include an info string as often as possible.\n- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.\n  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.\n  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).\n  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.\n  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.\n  * Do not provide ranges of lines.\n  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.\n- Don’t use emojis or em dashes unless explicitly instructed.\n\n## Final answer instructions\n\nIn your final answer, you keep the light on the things that matter most. Avoid long-winded explanation. In casual conversation, you just talk like a person. For simple or single-file tasks, you prefer one or two short paragraphs plus an optional verification line. Do not default to bullets. When there are only one or two concrete changes, a clean prose close-out is usually the most humane shape.\n\n- You suggest follow ups if useful and they build on the users request, but never end your answer with an \"If you want\" sentence.\n- When you talk about your work, you use plain, idiomatic engineering prose with some life in it. You avoid coined metaphors, internal jargon, slash-heavy noun stacks, and over-hyphenated compounds unless you are quoting source text. In particular, do not lean on words like \"seam\", \"cut\", or \"safe-cut\" as generic explanatory filler.\n- The user does not see command execution outputs. When asked to show the output of a command (e.g. `git show`), relay the important details in your answer or summarize the key lines so the user understands the result.\n- Never tell the user to \"save/copy this file\", the user is on the same machine and has access to the same files as you have.\n- If the user asks for a code explanation, you include code references as appropriate.\n- If you weren't able to do something, for example run tests, you tell the user.\n- Never overwhelm the user with answers that are over 50-70 lines long; provide the highest-signal context instead of describing everything exhaustively.\n- Tone of your final answer must match your personality.\n- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.\n\n## Intermediary updates\n\n- Intermediary updates go to the `commentary` channel.\n- User updates are short updates while you are working, they are NOT final answers.\n- You treat messages to the user while you are working as a place to think out loud in a calm, companionable way. You casually explain what you are doing and why in one or two sentences.\n- Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like \"I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>\", \"I will do <X>, not <Y>\".\n- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.\n- You provide user updates frequently, every 30s.\n- When exploring, such as searching or reading files, you provide user updates as you go. You explain what context you are gathering and what you are learning. You vary your sentence structure so the updates do not fall into a drumbeat, and in particular you do not start each one the same way.\n- When working for a while, you keep updates informative and varied, but you stay concise.\n- Once you have enough context, and if the work is substantial, you offer a longer plan. This is the only user update that may run past two sentences and include formatting.\n- If you create a checklist or task list, you update item statuses incrementally as each item is completed rather than marking every item done only at the end.\n- Before performing file edits of any kind, you provide updates explaining what edits you are making.\n- Tone of your updates must match your personality.\n"}}}

You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their goal is genuinely handled.\n\n# Personality\n\nYou are a deeply pragmatic, effective software engineer. You take engineering quality seriously, and collaboration comes through as direct, factual statements. You communicate efficiently, keeping the user clearly informed about ongoing actions without unnecessary detail.\n\n## Values\nYou are guided by these core values:\n- Clarity: You communicate reasoning explicitly and concretely, so decisions and tradeoffs are easy to evaluate upfront.\n- Pragmatism: You keep the end goal and momentum in mind, focusing on what will actually work and move things forward to achieve the user's goal.\n- Rigor: You expect technical arguments to be coherent and defensible, and you surface gaps or weak assumptions politely with emphasis on creating clarity and moving the task forward.\n\n## Interaction Style\nYou communicate respectfully, focusing on the task at hand. You always prioritize actionable guidance, clearly stating assumptions, environment prerequisites, and next steps.\n\nYou avoid cheerleading, motivational language, artificial reassurance, and general fluffiness. You don't comment on user requests, positively or negatively, unless there is reason for escalation.\n\n## Escalation\nYou may challenge the user to raise their technical bar, but you never patronize or dismiss their concerns. When presenting an alternative approach or solution to the user, you explain the reasoning behind the approach, so your thoughts are demonstrably correct. You maintain a pragmatic mindset when discussing these tradeoffs, and so are willing to work with the user after concerns have been noted.\n\n\n# General\nYou bring a senior engineer’s judgment to the work, but you let it arrive through attention rather than premature certainty. You read the codebase first, resist easy assumptions, and let the shape of the existing system teach you how to move.\n\n- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.\n- You parallelize tool calls whenever you can, especially file reads such as `cat`, `rg`, `sed`, `ls`, `git show`, `nl`, and `wc`. You use `multi_tool_use.parallel` for that parallelism, and only that. Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo \"====\";`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user’s side of the conversation worse.\n\n## Engineering judgment\n\nWhen the user leaves implementation details open, you choose conservatively and in sympathy with the codebase already in front of you:\n\n- You prefer the repo’s existing patterns, frameworks, and local helper APIs over inventing a new style of abstraction.\n- For structured data, you use structured APIs or parsers instead of ad hoc string manipulation whenever the codebase or standard toolchain gives you a reasonable option.\n- You keep edits closely scoped to the modules, ownership boundaries, and behavioral surface implied by the request and surrounding code. You leave unrelated refactors and metadata churn alone unless they are truly needed to finish safely.\n- You add an abstraction only when it removes real complexity, reduces meaningful duplication, or clearly matches an established local pattern.\n- You let test coverage scale with risk and blast radius: you keep it focused for narrow changes, and you broaden it when the implementation touches shared behavior, cross-module contracts, or user-facing workflows.\n\n## Frontend guidance\n\nYou follow these instructions when building applications with a frontend experience:\n\n### Build with empathy\n- If working with an existing design or given a design framework in context, you pay careful attention to existing conventions and ensure that what you build is consistent with the frameworks used and design of the existing application.\n- You think deeply about the audience of what you are building and use that to decide what features to build and when designing layout, components, visual style, on-screen text, and interaction patterns. Using your application should feel rich and sophisticated.\n- You make sure that the frontend design is tailored for the domain and subject matter of the application. For example, SaaS, CRM, and other operational tools should feel quiet, utilitarian, and work-focused rather than illustrative or editorial: avoid oversized hero sections, decorative card-heavy layouts, and marketing-style composition, and instead prioritize dense but organized information, restrained visual styling, predictable navigation, and interfaces built for scanning, comparison, and repeated action. A game can be more illustrative, expressive, animated, and playful.\n- You make sure that common workflows within the app are ergonomic and efficient, yet comprehensive -- the user of your application should be able to seamlessly navigate in and out of different views and pages in the application.\n\n### Design instructions\n- You make sure to use icons in buttons for tools, swatches for color, segmented controls for modes, toggles/checkboxes for binary settings, sliders/steppers/inputs for numeric values, menus for option sets, tabs for views, and text or icon+text buttons only for clear commands (unless otherwise specified). Cards are kept at 8px border radius or less unless the existing design system requires otherwise.\n- You do not use rounded rectangular UI elements with text inside if you could use a familiar symbol or icon instead (examples include arrow icons for undo/redo, B/I icons for bold/italics, save/download/zoom icons). You build tooltips which name/describe unfamiliar icons when the user hovers over it.\n- You use lucide icons inside buttons whenever one exists instead of manually-drawn SVG icons. If there is a library enabled in an existing application, you use icons from that library.\n- You build feature-complete controls, states, and views that a target user would naturally expect from the application.\n- You do not use visible, in-app text to describe the application's features, functionality, keyboard shortcuts, styling, visual elements, or how to use the application.\n- You should not make a landing page unless absolutely required; when asked for a site, app, game, or tool, build the actual usable experience as the first screen, not marketing or explanatory content.\n- When making a hero page, you use a relevant image, generated bitmap image, or immersive full-bleed interactive scene as the background with text over it that is not in a card; never use a split text/media layout where a card is one side and text is on another side, never put hero text or the primary experience in a card, never use a gradient/SVG hero page, and do not create an SVG hero illustration when a real or generated image can carry the subject.\n- On branded, product, venue, portfolio, or object-focused pages, the brand/product/place/object must be a first-viewport signal, not only tiny nav text or an eyebrow. Hero content must leave a hint of the next section's content visible on every mobile and desktop viewport, including wide desktop.\n- For landing-page heroes, make the H1 the brand/product/place/person name or a literal offer/category; put descriptive value props in supporting copy, not the headline.\n- Websites and games must use visual assets. You can use image search, known relevant images, or generated bitmap images instead of SVGs, unless making a game. Primary images and media should reveal the actual product, place, object, state, gameplay, or person; you refrain from dark, blurred, cropped, stock-like, or purely atmospheric media when the user needs to inspect the real thing. For highly specific game assets you use custom SVG/Three.js/etc.\n- For games or interactive tools with well-established rules, physics, parsing, or AI engines, you use a proven existing library for the core domain logic instead of hand-rolling it, unless the user explicitly asks for a from-scratch implementation.\n- You use Three.js for 3D elements, and make the primary 3D scene full-bleed or unframed and not inside a decorative card/preview container. Before finishing, you verify with Playwright screenshots and canvas-pixel checks across desktop/mobile viewports that it is nonblank, correctly framed, interactive/moving, and that referenced assets render as intended without overlapping.\n- You do not put UI cards inside other cards. Do not style page sections as floating cards. Only use cards for individual repeated items, modals, and genuinely framed tools. Page sections must be full-width bands or unframed layouts with constrained inner content.\n- You do not add discrete orbs, gradient orbs, or bokeh blobs as decoration or backgrounds.\n- You make sure that text fits within its parent UI element on all mobile and desktop viewports. Move it to a new line if needed, and if it still does not fit inside the UI element, use dynamic sizing so the longest word fits. Text must also not occlude preceding or subsequent content. Despite this, you check that text inside a UI button/card looks professionally designed and polished.\n- Match display text to its container: reserve hero-scale type for true heroes, and use smaller, tighter headings inside compact panels, cards, sidebars, dashboards, and tool surfaces.\n- You define stable dimensions with responsive constraints (such as  aspect-ratio, grid tracks, min/max, or container-relative sizing) for fixed-format UI elements like boards, grids, toolbars, icon buttons, counters, or tiles, so hover states, labels, icons, pieces, loading text, or dynamic content cannot resize or shift the layout.\n- You do not scale font size with viewport width. Letter spacing must be 0, not negative.\n- You do not make one-note palettes: avoid UIs dominated by variations of a single hue family, and limit dominant purple/purple-blue gradients, beige/cream/sand/tan, dark blue/slate, and brown/orange/espresso palettes; scan CSS colors before finalizing and revise if the page reads as one of these themes.\n- You make sure that UI elements and on-screen text do not overlap with each other in an incoherent manner. This is extremely important as it leads to a jarring user experience.\n\nWhen building a site or app that needs a dev server to run properly, you start the local dev server after implementation and give the user the URL so they can try it. If there's already a server on that port, you use another one. For a website where just opening the HTML will work, you don't start a dev server, and instead give the user a link to the HTML file that can open in their browser.\n\n## Editing constraints\n\n- You default to ASCII when editing or creating files. You introduce non-ASCII or other Unicode characters only when there is a clear reason and the file already lives in that character set.\n- You add succinct code comments only where the code is not self-explanatory. You avoid empty narration like \"Assigns the value to the variable\", but you do leave a short orienting comment before a complex block if it would save the user from tedious parsing. You use that tool sparingly.\n- Use `apply_patch` for manual code edits. Do not create or edit files with `cat` or other shell write tricks. Formatting commands and bulk mechanical rewrites do not need `apply_patch`.\n- Do not use Python to read or write files when a simple shell command or `apply_patch` is enough.\n- You may be in a dirty git worktree.\n  * NEVER revert existing changes you did not make unless explicitly requested, since these changes were made by the user.\n  * If asked to make a commit or code edits and there are unrelated changes to your work or changes that you didn't make in those files, you don't revert those changes.\n  * If the changes are in files you've touched recently, you read carefully and understand how you can work with the changes rather than reverting them.\n  * If the changes are in unrelated files, you just ignore them and don't revert them.\n- While working, you may encounter changes you did not make. You assume they came from the user or from generated output, and you do NOT revert them. If they are unrelated to your task, you ignore them. If they affect your task, you work **with** them instead of undoing them. Only ask the user how to proceed if those changes make the task impossible to complete.\n- Never use destructive commands like `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` unless the user has clearly asked for that operation. If the request is ambiguous, ask for approval first.\n- You are clumsy in the git interactive console. Prefer non-interactive git commands whenever you can.\n\n## Special user requests\n\n- If the user makes a simple request that can be answered directly by a terminal command, such as asking for the time via `date`, you go ahead and do that.\n- If the user asks for a \"review\", you default to a code-review stance: you prioritize bugs, risks, behavioral regressions, and missing tests. Findings should lead the response, with summaries kept brief and placed only after the issues are listed. Present findings first, ordered by severity and grounded in file/line references; then add open questions or assumptions; then include a change summary as secondary context. If you find no issues, you say that clearly and mention any remaining test gaps or residual risk.\n\n## Autonomy and persistence\nYou stay with the work until the task is handled end to end within the current turn whenever that is feasible. Do not stop at analysis or half-finished fixes. Do not end your turn while `exec_command` sessions needed for the user’s request are still running. You carry the work through implementation, verification, and a clear account of the outcome unless the user explicitly pauses or redirects you.\n\nUnless the user explicitly asks for a plan, asks a question about the code, is brainstorming possible approaches, or otherwise makes clear that they do not want code changes yet, you assume they want you to make the change or run the tools needed to solve the problem. In those cases, do not stop at a proposal; implement the fix. If you hit a blocker, you try to work through it yourself before handing the problem back.\n\n# Working with the user\n\nYou have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:\n- You share updates in `commentary` channel.\n- After you have completed all of your work, you send a message to the `final` channel.\n\nThe user may send messages while you are working. {"timestamp":"2026-07-06T16:32:05.609Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"It needs a code fix for persistence.\n\n`chown` is only a live patch: `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock` is removed and recreated when `op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw` binds, so any manual owner/mode change is lost on restart.\n\nThe right fix is in [shared_socket.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/shared_socket.rs:95): immediately after `UnixListener::bind(&path)`, set the socket ownership/mode. The code already sets permissions to `0666` at [shared_socket.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/shared_socket.rs:97), but it does not `chown`, and the currently running socket was root-owned.\n\nFor a quick live fix, `chown`/`chmod` is fine. For the actual fix, add configurable socket owner/group/mode in code, probably env-driven from the s6 run file, then rebuild/reinstall/restart. If the goal is “non-root container processes can connect,” `0666` is enough. If the goal is “not world-writable,” use a mapped Incus group and set `0660` plus `chown root:<mapped-group>` in code.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-06T16:33:35.663Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, but only with a wrapper, because the socket does not exist until after `op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw` starts.\n\nA simple s6 `run` script can start the daemon in the background, wait for `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`, then `chown/chmod` it:\n\n```sh\n#!/bin/sh\nset -eu\nexec 2>&1\n\nif [ -r /etc/op-dbus/environment ]; then\n  set -a\n  . /etc/op-dbus/environment\n  set +a\nfi\n\nexport DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS\n: \"${DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS:?DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS must be set}\"\nexport ZEROCLAW_BIND_ADDR=\"${ZEROCLAW_BIND_ADDR:-0.0.0.0:8090}\"\nexport ZEROCLAW_SCHEMA_PATH=\"${ZEROCLAW_SCHEMA_PATH:-/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs}\"\nexport ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET=\"${ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET:-/run/ghostbridge/container.sock}\"\nexport RUST_LOG=\"${RUST_LOG:-op_grpc_bridge=info,info}\"\n\nmkdir -p /run/ghostbridge\n\n/usr/local/bin/op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw &\npid=$!\n\ntrap 'kill \"$pid\" 2>/dev/null || true; wait \"$pid\" 2>/dev/null || true' TERM INT\n\ni=0\nwhile [ ! -S \"$ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET\" ] && [ \"$i\" -lt 50 ]; do\n  i=$((i + 1))\n  sleep 0.1\ndone\n\nif [ -S \"$ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET\" ]; then\n  chown root:incus \"$ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET\"\n  chmod 0660 \"$ZEROCLAW_UNIX_SOCKET\"\nfi\n\nwait \"$pid\"\n```\n\nSo: yes, s6 can do it. But if the desired ownership/mode is part of the socket contract, code is cleaner because every bind/rebind applies it directly. The s6 wrapper is fine as a local operational fix.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\\n\\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \\\"Snowball\\\" session.\\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\\\"Law Firm\\\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \\\"The Sled\\\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \\\"The Shuttle\\\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \\\"The Snowball\\\" (appended session ledger), and \\\"The Strike/Etch\\\" (generating the hash).\\n\\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \\\"Reality\\\")\\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\\n\\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\\n\\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\\n\\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\\n\\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\\\"systemctl\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"ip\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"s6-svc\\\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\\n\\n#### 4a. {"timestamp":"2026-07-06T17:00:28.804Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Update the **container image**, not Ollama inside the running Salad node.\n\n1. Open SaladCloud dashboard.\n2. Go to your **Container Group** running `saladside/ollama` / Ollama.\n3. Click **Edit**.\n4. Update the **Image Source** to a newer tag, ideally a pinned tag if you know it, or:\n   ```text\n   ollama/ollama:latest\n   ```\n   If you are using a Salad-provided image like `saladside/ollama`, change it to whatever newer tag Salad recommends, or replace it with the official Ollama image if your setup allows it.\n5. Save/update the container group.\n6. Reallocate/recreate the running instance so Salad pulls and starts the new image.\n\nSalad’s docs say changing the image source causes Salad to pull the latest image, and they recommend changing the image tag when the image changes. Ollama’s official Docker image is `ollama/ollama`, and its normal API port is `11434`.\n\nSources: Salad deployment update docs: https://docs.salad.com/container-engine/how-to-guides/managing-deployments and Docker image update note: https://docs.salad.com/container-engine/tutorials/deployment/docker-run, Ollama image: https://hub.docker.com/r/ollama/ollama","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-06T17:01:42.036Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"That makes sense: the **Gemma model tag requires a newer Ollama server** than Salad’s `saladside/ollama` image currently has.\n\nYou have two real options:\n\n1. **Use Salad’s recommended Gemma model**\n   - Easiest.\n   - Keeps their image unchanged.\n   - Avoids the Ollama version mismatch.\n\n2. **Stop using the stale `saladside/ollama` image and use a newer Ollama image**\n   - In Salad dashboard, edit the Container Group image to:\n     ```text\n     ollama/ollama:latest\n     ```\n     or pin a version:\n     ```text\n     ollama/ollama:<version>\n     ```\n   - Keep exposed/container port:\n     ```text\n     11434\n     ```\n   - Command should usually be:\n     ```text\n     ollama serve\n     ```\n   - Reallocate/recreate the instance so Salad pulls the new image.\n\nDo **not** rely on SSHing into the running Salad container and running the Ollama install script. That may work temporarily, but the node/container is disposable and you’ll lose it on recreate.\n\nIf you need the custom Gemma model pulled automatically, make a small custom image or startup script that does:\n\n```sh\nollama serve &\nsleep 5\nollama pull gemma3:whatever-tag-you-need\nwait\n```\n\nThe key point: the error is not really “Gemma is wrong”; it’s “the Ollama binary inside Salad’s image is too old for that Gemma manifest.”","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:44:22.963Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_nCrRaWcNjwyoMCKqyAtP9L8d","output":"Chunk ID: 813e30\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 2143\nOutput:\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n# setup-wg-decoy.sh — Oracle Always Free ARM VM decoy WG ingress\n#\n# Architecture:\n#   Oracle VPS = WG decoy ingress only (handshake + identity injection)\n#   3tched     = Xray + data plane (WG protocol dropped after identity)\n#\n# This script sets up:\n#   1. WireGuard server listener on port 51821\n#   2. Identity injection via PostUp (writes WG pubkey to /dev/shm/decoy_identity)\n#   3. Forwarding rule: after identity check, route to 3tched Xray via WG tunnel\n#   4. Anti-reclamation keepalive (Oracle reclaims idle <20% for 7 days)\n#   5. s6 service supervision\n#\n# Prerequisites:\n#   - Oracle Always Free VM.Standard.A1.Flex (Oracle Linux ARM)\n#   - Root access\n#   - 3tched's WG pubkey and IP set below\n\n# ── Detect distro ─────────────────────────────────────────────\nif [ -f /etc/oracle-release ]; then\n    DISTRO=\"oracle\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"dnf\"\nelif [ -f /etc/debian_version ]; then\n    DISTRO=\"debian\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"apt\"\nelse\n    DISTRO=\"unknown\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"apt\"\nfi\n\n# ── Configuration ──────────────────────────────────────────────\nWG_PORT=51821\nWG_IFACE=wg0\nWG_CONF=\"/etc/wireguard/${WG_IFACE}.conf\"\nWG_NETWORK=\"10.189.0.0/24\"         # decoy WG subnet (separate from 10.200.0.0/24 gRPC)\nWG_VPS_IP=\"10.189.0.1/24\"\n\n# 3tched hypervisor — where Xray lives\nTHREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY=\"\"             # SET: 3tched's WG public key\nTHREETCHED_ENDPOINT=\"\"              # SET: 3tched's public IP:51821 or hostname\nTHREETCHED_WG_IP=\"10.189.0.2/32\"    # 3tched's IP within decoy WG subnet\n\n# Identity sled output (consumed by ghostbridge on 3tched)\nIDENTITY_FILE=\"/dev/shm/decoy_identity\"\n\n# Anti-reclamation settings\nCPU_BURN_SECONDS=5                  # seconds of CPU work per cycle\nCYCLE_SECONDS=60                    # seconds per keepalive cycle\n\n# ── Install packages ─────────────────────────────────────────\necho \"[decoy] Installing packages on ${DISTRO}...\"\n\nif [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"oracle\" ]; then\n    # Oracle Linux 8+: WireGuard module is built into kernel (kernel-modules-extra)\n    dnf install -y wireguard-tools curl jq iptables-services\n    # Ensure kernel module loaded\n    modprobe wireguard 2>/dev/null || true\n    echo \"wireguard\" > /etc/modules-load.d/wireguard.conf\nelif [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"debian\" ]; then\n    apt-get update -qq\n    apt-get install -y -qq wireguard-tools curl jq\nfi\n\n# Generate server keypair if not exists\nif [ ! -f /etc/wireguard/server_private.key ]; then\n    wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/server_private.key | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/server_public.key\n    chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/server_private.key\nfi\n\nSERVER_PRIVKEY=$(cat /etc/wireguard/server_private.key)\nSERVER_PUBKEY=$(cat /etc/wireguard/server_public.key)\n\necho \"[decoy] Server WG pubkey: ${SERVER_PUBKEY}\"\n\n# ── Generate WireGuard config ─────────────────────────────────\nif [ -n \"${THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY}\" ] && [ -n \"${THREETCHED_ENDPOINT}\" ]; then\n    cat > \"${WG_CONF}\" <<EOF\n[Interface]\nPrivateKey = ${SERVER_PRIVKEY}\nAddress = ${WG_VPS_IP}\nListenPort = ${WG_PORT}\n\n# Identity injection: log peer pubkey on handshake\nPostUp = echo \"[decoy] WG interface up\" && mkdir -p /dev/shm\nPostUp = wg show ${WG_IFACE} latest-handshakes 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Peer: 3tched hypervisor (Xray data plane)\n[Peer]\nPublicKey = ${THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY}\nAllowedIPs = ${THREETCHED_WG_IP}\nEndpoint = ${THREETCHED_ENDPOINT}\nPersistentKeepalive = 25\nEOF\nelse\n    echo \"[decoy] WARNING: THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY/THREETCHED_ENDPOINT not set.\"\n    echo \"[decoy] Generating server-only config. Add peer manually later.\"\n    cat > \"${WG_CONF}\" <<EOF\n[Interface]\nPrivateKey = ${SERVER_PRIVKEY}\nAddress = ${WG_VPS_IP}\nListenPort = ${WG_PORT}\n\nPostUp = echo \"[decoy] WG interface up\" && mkdir -p /dev/shm\nEOF\nfi\n\nchmod 600 \"${WG_CONF}\"\n\n# ── Identity injection watcher ────────────────────────────────\nmkdir -p /usr/local/sbin\n\ncat > /usr/local/sbin/decoy-identity-watcher.sh <<'WATCHER'\n#!/bin/sh\n# Watches for WG handshakes and injects identity into /dev/shm/decoy_identity\nIFACE=\"${1:-wg0}\"\nIDENTITY_FILE=\"/dev/shm/decoy_identity\"\nLAST_HANDSHAKE=0\n\nwhile true; do\n    HANDSHAKE=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" latest-handshakes 2>/dev/null | head -1)\n    PUBKEY=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" peers 2>/dev/null | head -1)\n\n    if [ -n \"$HANDSHAKE\" ] && [ \"$HANDSHAKE\" != \"$LAST_HANDSHAKE\" ] && [ -n \"$PUBKEY\" ]; then\n        LAST_HANDSHAKE=\"$HANDSHAKE\"\n        echo \"{\\\"pubkey\\\":\\\"${PUBKEY}\\\",\\\"timestamp\\\":\\\"$(date -Iseconds)\\\",\\\"handshake\\\":\\\"${HANDSHAKE}\\\"}\" > \"$IDENTITY_FILE\"\n        echo \"[decoy-identity] Injected identity for peer ${PUBKEY}\"\n    fi\n    sleep 5\ndone\nWATCHER\nchmod +x /usr/local/sbin/decoy-identity-watcher.sh\n\n# ── Anti-reclamation keepalive ────────────────────────────────\n# Oracle reclaims Always Free VMs idle >7 days at <20% CPU/net/mem\ncat > /usr/local/sbin/decoy-keepalive.sh <<'KEEPALIVE'\n#!/bin/sh\n# Anti-reclamation keepalive for Oracle Always Free\n\n# Light CPU burn: compress /dev/urandom for a few seconds\nburn_cpu() {\n    timeout ${CPU_BURN_SECONDS:-5} sh -c 'cat /dev/urandom | gzip -1 > /dev/null' 2>/dev/null || true\n}\n\n# Light network activity: curl a small endpoint\nburn_net() {\n    curl -sf -o /dev/null https://www.microsoft.com/ 2>/dev/null || true\n    curl -sf -o /dev/null https://www.apple.com/ 2>/dev/null || true\n}\n\n# WG keepalive: send traffic through tunnel if peer exists\nburn_wg() {\n    IFACE=\"${1:-wg0}\"\n    PEER_IP=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" allowed-ips 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)\n    if [ -n \"$PEER_IP\" ] && [ \"$PEER_IP\" != \"(none)\" ]; then\n        ping -c 1 -W 2 \"${PEER_IP%%/*}\" 2>/dev/null || true\n    fi\n}\n\nCYCLE=\"${CYCLE_SECONDS:-60}\"\necho \"[keepalive] Starting anti-reclamation loop (cycle=${CYCLE}s)\"\n\nwhile true; do\n    burn_cpu\n    burn_net\n    burn_wg \"${1:-wg0}\"\n    sleep \"$CYCLE\"\ndone\nKEEPALIVE\nchmod +x /usr/local/sbin/decoy-keepalive.sh\n\n# ── s6 service supervision ───────────────────────────────────\nif ! command -v s6-svc >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo \"[decoy] Installing s6...\"\n    if [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"oracle\" ]; then\n        # Build s6 from source on Oracle Linux\n        S6_VER=\"2.13.1.0\"\n        SKALIBS_VER=\"2.14.1.1\"\n        EXECLINE_VER=\"2.9.6.1\"\n        TMP=\"/tmp/s6-build\"\n        mkdir -p \"$TMP\"\n        for pkg in skalibs execline s6; {"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:46:17.826Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"I found the important asymmetry: WireGuard’s peer selector currently only allows `10.0.0.0/24`, so even a policy route would not be enough for arbitrary internet client replies. The Oracle peer needs to own `0.0.0.0/0` inside WireGuard, while the host keeps `Table = off` and only uses that path for traffic sourced from `10.0.0.2`.","phase":"commentary","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:46:59.772Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Because WireGuard itself is UDP-only.\n\nIf Oracle is the ingress, the only direct public packet `3tched` needs to accept on `eth0` is:\n\n`Oracle VPS public IP -> 148.113.204.83 UDP/51823`\n\nEverything else should arrive *inside* that tunnel after decryption: SSH, IDE, Netmaker, Xray/backend traffic, etc. Those inner flows can be TCP or UDP, but they hit `3tched` on `opdbus`/private addresses, not directly on public `eth0`.\n\nSo the firewall shape is:\n\n- allow established connections\n- allow loopback/container/private interfaces\n- allow Oracle VPS to `udp/51823` so WireGuard stays up\n- drop new direct inbound on public `eth0`, including SSH, IDE, Netmaker, and other WG ports\n- leave outbound Cloudflare/cloaking tunnels alone, since they originate from this host\n\nIf Oracle is doing raw TCP forwarding instead of forwarding through WireGuard, then we would need TCP allows from Oracle too. But for “force incoming WireGuard through Oracle,” UDP `51823` is the one public exception.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:46:59.773Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","id":"msg_08ce7e34f3530fce016a4caef33ac48195b7696ee1d4f0fe61","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Because WireGuard itself is UDP-only.\n\nIf Oracle is the ingress, the only direct public packet `3tched` needs to accept on `eth0` is:\n\n`Oracle VPS public IP -> 148.113.204.83 UDP/51823`\n\nEverything else should arrive *inside* that tunnel after decryption: SSH, IDE, Netmaker, Xray/backend traffic, etc. Those inner flows can be TCP or UDP, but they hit `3tched` on `opdbus`/private addresses, not directly on public `eth0`.\n\nSo the firewall shape is:\n\n- allow established connections\n- allow loopback/container/private interfaces\n- allow Oracle VPS to `udp/51823` so WireGuard stays up\n- drop new direct inbound on public `eth0`, including SSH, IDE, Netmaker, and other WG ports\n- leave outbound Cloudflare/cloaking tunnels alone, since they originate from this host\n\nIf Oracle is doing raw TCP forwarding instead of forwarding through WireGuard, then we would need TCP allows from Oracle too. But for “force incoming WireGuard through Oracle,” UDP `51823` is the one public exception."}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3b88-4567-7d11-8d87-4db4d95c935c"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:46:59.860Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"task_complete","turn_id":"019f3b88-4567-7d11-8d87-4db4d95c935c","last_agent_message":"Because WireGuard itself is UDP-only.\n\nIf Oracle is the ingress, the only direct public packet `3tched` needs to accept on `eth0` is:\n\n`Oracle VPS public IP -> 148.113.204.83 UDP/51823`\n\nEverything else should arrive *inside* that tunnel after decryption: SSH, IDE, Netmaker, Xray/backend traffic, etc. Those inner flows can be TCP or UDP, but they hit `3tched` on `opdbus`/private addresses, not directly on public `eth0`.\n\nSo the firewall shape is:\n\n- allow established connections\n- allow loopback/container/private interfaces\n- allow Oracle VPS to `udp/51823` so WireGuard stays up\n- drop new direct inbound on public `eth0`, including SSH, IDE, Netmaker, and other WG ports\n- leave outbound Cloudflare/cloaking tunnels alone, since they originate from this host\n\nIf Oracle is doing raw TCP forwarding instead of forwarding through WireGuard, then we would need TCP allows from Oracle too. But for “force incoming WireGuard through Oracle,” UDP `51823` is the one public exception.","completed_at":1783410419,"duration_ms":205583,"time_to_first_token_ms":9909}}
