{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:50:15.248Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, but only for the tunnel side.\n\n`/etc/wireguard/opdbus.conf` and `wg-decoy.conf` determine which peer this host talks to, what `AllowedIPs` are reachable through that tunnel, and which local port WireGuard listens on. The public entry point itself lives on the Oracle side: that VPS’s server config is what accepts inbound WG on `129.153.134.63:51821`.\n\nSo on this machine:\n- `opdbus.conf` is the local client profile for the Oracle tunnel\n- `wg-decoy.conf` is another local client profile pointed at the same Oracle endpoint\n- the Oracle VPS config is the actual ingress gate\n\nIf you want the main server to stay dark except for the cloaking path, the WG config alone is not enough unless it also carries `PostUp`/`PostDown` rules for the `eth0` ingress filter. That is the right place to express it if you want to keep the change inside the WG config layer.\n\n","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":{"entries":[{"path":"MEMORY.md","lineStart":321,"lineEnd":347,"note":"oracle wireguard topology and decoy ingress context"}],"rolloutIds":[]}}}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:50:15.248Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","id":"msg_0cb7b6c4fa1f8948016a4cafb898308193941bd2e2bf399b08","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Yes, but only for the tunnel side.\n\n`/etc/wireguard/opdbus.conf` and `wg-decoy.conf` determine which peer this host talks to, what `AllowedIPs` are reachable through that tunnel, and which local port WireGuard listens on. The public entry point itself lives on the Oracle side: that VPS’s server config is what accepts inbound WG on `129.153.134.63:51821`.\n\nSo on this machine:\n- `opdbus.conf` is the local client profile for the Oracle tunnel\n- `wg-decoy.conf` is another local client profile pointed at the same Oracle endpoint\n- the Oracle VPS config is the actual ingress gate\n\nIf you want the main server to stay dark except for the cloaking path, the WG config alone is not enough unless it also carries `PostUp`/`PostDown` rules for the `eth0` ingress filter. That is the right place to express it if you want to keep the change inside the WG config layer.\n\n<oai-mem-citation>\n<citation_entries>\nMEMORY.md:321-347|note=[oracle wireguard topology and decoy ingress context]\n</citation_entries>\n<rollout_ids>\n</rollout_ids>\n</oai-mem-citation>"}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3b8b-b485-7dc3-8ee1-2591328b5752"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:52:42.307Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"No. `fwmark` is not an IP, and it does not by itself send traffic anywhere.\n\nWhat it does is tag packets with a numeric mark. Then `ip rule` can match that mark and send the packet into a routing table whose default route points where you want.\n\nSo the workable shape is:\n\n1. Mark packets from the traffic you want to force.\n2. Add an `ip rule` for that mark.\n3. Put a default route in that table that points at the hypervisor/Xray path.\n4. Make sure Xray’s own control traffic does not get caught in the same rule, or you create a loop.\n\nImportant detail: if the hypervisor is the actual Reality endpoint, you still need a real route to reach it. The mark does not replace routing. It only selects which routing table to use.\n\nSo:\n- `fwmark = 0x1` is valid\n- `fwmark = <xray server IP>` is not valid\n- “everything leaves there” only if the policy route is complete and not recursive\n\nFor your setup, the safer pattern is usually:\n- keep Oracle as the WG ingress\n- keep `3tched` as the local tunnel client\n- mark only the outbound flows that should use the Reality/Xray path\n- route those marked packets through the table that reaches the hypervisor Xray server\n- leave the tunnel control plane unmarked so the path stays up\n\nIf you want, I can map this into exact `wg` and `ip rule` lines for your current interfaces.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:52:42.321Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","id":"msg_0cb7b6c4fa1f8948016a4cb048066881938e7f25ee8904a0c6","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"No. `fwmark` is not an IP, and it does not by itself send traffic anywhere.\n\nWhat it does is tag packets with a numeric mark. Then `ip rule` can match that mark and send the packet into a routing table whose default route points where you want.\n\nSo the workable shape is:\n\n1. Mark packets from the traffic you want to force.\n2. Add an `ip rule` for that mark.\n3. Put a default route in that table that points at the hypervisor/Xray path.\n4. Make sure Xray’s own control traffic does not get caught in the same rule, or you create a loop.\n\nImportant detail: if the hypervisor is the actual Reality endpoint, you still need a real route to reach it. The mark does not replace routing. It only selects which routing table to use.\n\nSo:\n- `fwmark = 0x1` is valid\n- `fwmark = <xray server IP>` is not valid\n- “everything leaves there” only if the policy route is complete and not recursive\n\nFor your setup, the safer pattern is usually:\n- keep Oracle as the WG ingress\n- keep `3tched` as the local tunnel client\n- mark only the outbound flows that should use the Reality/Xray path\n- route those marked packets through the table that reaches the hypervisor Xray server\n- leave the tunnel control plane unmarked so the path stays up\n\nIf you want, I can map this into exact `wg` and `ip rule` lines for your current interfaces."}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3b90-581f-7fa3-a14d-98e811179827"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:52:55.115Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If that second IP is the hypervisor/Xray host, yes, it belongs in the routing path, but not as the `fwmark`.\n\nUse it as one of these, depending on what role it plays:\n\n- `Endpoint = <second-ip>:<port>` if it is the peer you dial\n- `AllowedIPs = <second-ip>/32` if you want the kernel to send only that host through the tunnel\n- `ip route add default via <second-ip> table <mark-table>` if it is the next hop for the policy-routed table\n\n`fwmark` itself should stay a small numeric tag like `0x1`. The IP goes in the route or peer config, not in the mark.\n\nIf you want, I can translate that into the exact `wg-quick` `PostUp` lines for your current `opdbus.conf`.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:54:27.440Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. The port belongs in the peer `Endpoint`, and it should match the WireGuard server `ListenPort`.\n\nSo if the WG server uses a random UDP port, the client should use:\n\n```ini\n[Peer]\nEndpoint = <server-ip>:<that-same-port>\n```\n\nand the server should have:\n\n```ini\n[Interface]\nListenPort = <that-same-port>\n```\n\nThat is the only place the port number matters for the WG link itself. If you change the WG server port, you must update:\n- the server `ListenPort`\n- the client `Endpoint`\n- any firewall/NAT rule that allows that UDP port\n\nIf you’re talking about the hypervisor/Xray side, that port is separate from the WG port. The WG port is just transport, not the Reality service port.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:55:46.859Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, if it’s a different server, the ports do not need to match.\n\nEach WireGuard peer just dials whatever `Endpoint = ip:port` that server is actually listening on. So this is fine:\n\n- decoy server: `ListenPort = 51821`\n- hypervisor egress server: `ListenPort = 51845`\n- client to decoy: `Endpoint = decoy-ip:51821`\n- client to hypervisor: `Endpoint = hypervisor-ip:51845`\n\nYou can also run two WG interfaces on the hypervisor if you want separate roles:\n- one interface for the decoy side\n- one interface for the egress side\n\nThat is workable, but keep them isolated:\n- different interface names\n- different keys\n- different `ListenPort`s\n- different route tables or `Table = off` plus explicit policy routing\n\nThe one thing to avoid is making both interfaces compete for the same default route, or you’ll get path ambiguity and loops.\n\nSo the answer is: yes, two WG endpoints is a valid design, and no, the ports do not have to match across different servers.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:55:46.859Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","id":"msg_0cb7b6c4fa1f8948016a4cb10377448193bb0135c175ec9d23","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Yes, if it’s a different server, the ports do not need to match.\n\nEach WireGuard peer just dials whatever `Endpoint = ip:port` that server is actually listening on. So this is fine:\n\n- decoy server: `ListenPort = 51821`\n- hypervisor egress server: `ListenPort = 51845`\n- client to decoy: `Endpoint = decoy-ip:51821`\n- client to hypervisor: `Endpoint = hypervisor-ip:51845`\n\nYou can also run two WG interfaces on the hypervisor if you want separate roles:\n- one interface for the decoy side\n- one interface for the egress side\n\nThat is workable, but keep them isolated:\n- different interface names\n- different keys\n- different `ListenPort`s\n- different route tables or `Table = off` plus explicit policy routing\n\nThe one thing to avoid is making both interfaces compete for the same default route, or you’ll get path ambiguity and loops.\n\nSo the answer is: yes, two WG endpoints is a valid design, and no, the ports do not have to match across different servers."}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3b93-4821-7693-b9c5-4cc4af7179b2"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:57:28.463Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Right. Then no second WireGuard on the hypervisor.\n\nThe role split is:\n\n- Oracle decoy WG: the bouncer/escort. It receives the inbound tunnel and hands you off.\n- `3tched`: the car/driver. It takes the connection onward.\n- Hypervisor Xray/Reality: the valet. That is where the session has to land for Reality to work.\n\nSo the design is not “WG all the way through.” It is:\n\n1. incoming to Oracle over WG\n2. Oracle hands off to `3tched`\n3. `3tched` egresses to the hypervisor Xray Reality endpoint\n4. no extra WG interface on the hypervisor\n\nThat means the only WG config we should keep touching is the Oracle ingress and the `3tched` client side. The hypervisor side should stay Xray-only.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T07:59:44.475Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. That is the point of the design.\n\nA narrow protocol layer with one stable role does add trust because it reduces:\n\n- endpoint churn\n- service fan-out\n- routing ambiguity\n- the number of places identity can leak or be reinterpreted\n\nIf the protocol colocation stays fixed, the attack and failure surface stays small. The key pair is the only moving part at the boundary, and the meaning of the traffic does not get bounced across unrelated services before it reaches Xray and becomes gRPC.\n\nSo the engineering preference here is: one ingress identity path, one morphing point, one outbound protocol shape. That is the point of the design.\n\nA narrow protocol layer with one stable role does add trust because it reduces:\n\n- endpoint churn\n- service fan-out\n- routing ambiguity\n- the number of places identity can leak or be reinterpreted\n\nIf the protocol colocation stays fixed, the attack and failure surface stays small. The key pair is the only moving part at the boundary, and the meaning of the traffic does not get bounced across unrelated services before it reaches Xray and becomes gRPC.\n\nSo the engineering preference here is: one ingress identity path, one morphing point, one outbound protocol shape. That is cleaner than spreading the same flow across multiple peers or interfaces.","completed_at":1783411184,"duration_ms":5699,"time_to_first_token_ms":3656}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T08:01:29.299Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. The way to make the key’s validity unambiguous and the attack surface small is to pin one peer and make the rest of the config narrow:\n\n- fixed `PublicKey` for that one peer\n- optional `PresharedKey` on both sides for an extra cryptographic layer\n- exact `Endpoint = <single-ip>:<single-port>`\n- exact `AllowedIPs = <single tunnel IP>/32` unless you truly need a subnet\n- no extra fallback peers\n- no roaming endpoints\n- `Table = off` if you do not want WireGuard to invent routes for you\n\nWireGuard’s model is exactly that: peers are identified by public keys, endpoints are separate, and `AllowedIPs` is a distinct trust/routing control. The docs also say a pre-shared key can be mixed into the handshake as an additional layer. That is the closest thing to “very little room to hack it” that the protocol itself gives you.\n\nWhat it does not give you is absolute proof beyond “the peer completed a handshake with the correct private key, and optionally the correct preshared key.” If you want the public side even tighter, the host firewall should only accept the one UDP port from the Oracle IP and drop the rest.\n\nSources:\n- [WireGuard home](https://www.wireguard.com/)\n- [Quick Start](https://www.wireguard.com/quickstart/)\n- [Known Limitations](https://www.wireguard.com/known-limitations/)\n- [WireGuard whitepaper](https://www.wireguard.com/papers/wireguard.pdf)","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

The docs also say a pre-shared key can be mixed into the handshake as an additional layer. That is the closest thing to “very little room to hack it” that the protocol itself gives you.\n\nWhat it does not give you is absolute proof beyond “the peer completed a handshake with the correct private key, and optionally the correct preshared key.” If you want the public side even tighter, the host firewall should only accept the one UDP port from the Oracle IP and drop the rest.\n\nSources:\n- [WireGuard home](https://www.wireguard.com/)\n- [Quick Start](https://www.wireguard.com/quickstart/)\n- [Known Limitations](https://www.wireguard.com/known-limitations/)\n- [WireGuard whitepaper](https://www.wireguard.com/papers/wireguard.pdf)"}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3b98-3902-7370-8446-6c327f1b2b46"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T08:03:19.314Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. That is the cleaner boundary.\n\nDo not start sled inside the WireGuard leg. Let WireGuard do only identity-bearing ingress, then hand a small authenticated request to Xray on the VPS. Xray can then perform the injection locally on the VPS side, where the Reality/protocol morphing already lives.\n\nSo the split becomes:\n\n- WireGuard: proves the keypair and gets the request onto the VPS\n- Xray on the VPS: validates the request and performs the injection\n- sled: stays out of that path unless it is already part of the VPS-side control plane\n\nThat keeps the trust surface small and avoids putting stateful machinery inside the escort path. It also matches the one-endpoint invariant you wanted: the WG peer authenticates once, then Xray handles the rest on the VPS.\n\nIf you want to implement it cleanly, the right shape is a local control channel on the VPS between the WG-facing side and Xray, not a second tunnel and not sled in the ingress path.\n\n","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":{"entries":[{"path":"MEMORY.md","lineStart":321,"lineEnd":347,"note":"oracle decoy ingress is WG-only and the VPS is the handoff point"}],"rolloutIds":[]}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T08:03:45.717Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, if sled is started on the same machine and network namespace where the WireGuard interface is up, it can see that interface.\n\nWhat creates the interface is still WireGuard, not sled. So the rule is:\n\n- `wg-quick` or `wg` brings `wg0` up\n- sled can then use that local presence if it runs on the same host/netns\n- if sled runs in a different namespace or container, the interface is not automatically visible there\n\nSo if your idea is “start sled on the VPS and have Xray use the local WG-facing side,” that works only if sled lives in the same network namespace as the WG interface. It does not need to own the interface, but it can only use what is actually present in its namespace.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T08:05:29.424Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, with one caveat.\n\nIf Xray only receives the request after the packet has already been accepted and decrypted by the WireGuard side, then the request is downstream of a valid WG authentication event. In that sense, the WG confirmation is real and not arguable.\n\nWhat is not automatic is the trust on the handoff from the WG-facing layer into Xray. Xray should trust the local handoff only if that path is:\n- local to the VPS\n- bound to the authenticated WG peer identity\n- not forgeable by some other local process\n\nSo the clean statement is:\n\n- WireGuard proves the peer\n- Xray consumes the peer-authenticated request\n- Xray itself is not proving WireGuard, it is acting after WireGuard has already proven the peer\n\nThat is still a valid design. It just means the boundary is WG-authenticated input into Xray, not “Xray somehow validates WG on its own.”","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-08T02:46:00.443Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. That was the wrong layer to probe.\n\nIf all DNS records point at the decoy, then the host’s own resolver success only proves the box can resolve names for itself. It does not prove the public DNS path that matters for your setup, which is:\n\n- public DNS record points to the decoy\n- decoy receives the traffic\n- Gemma/Xray routes it to the right container\n\nSo the failure, if there is one, is more likely in one of these:\n- the authoritative DNS records still point somewhere unexpected\n- the decoy is not forwarding the request correctly\n- Gemma is not selecting the right container after the handoff\n\nI was checking the host resolver, which is not the decision point in your architecture. The useful next check is the decoy-facing path and the Gemma route mapping, not `/etc/resolv.conf` on the main box.\n\n","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":{"entries":[{"path":"MEMORY.md","lineStart":321,"lineEnd":347,"note":"oracle decoy ingress context for the WG/VPS handoff path"}],"rolloutIds":[]}}}

It does not prove the public DNS path that matters for your setup, which is:\n\n- public DNS record points to the decoy\n- decoy receives the traffic\n- Gemma/Xray routes it to the right container\n\nSo the failure, if there is one, is more likely in one of these:\n- the authoritative DNS records still point somewhere unexpected\n- the decoy is not forwarding the request correctly\n- Gemma is not selecting the right container after the handoff\n\nI was checking the host resolver, which is not the decision point in your architecture. {"timestamp":"2026-07-08T02:54:40.812Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_pzh0eMoLxRTP3qxDBOAGMiCP","output":"Chunk ID: 95221b\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 336\nOutput:\n  - GetAgentStatus(agent_id) → status_json\n\n- org.opdbus.Orchestrator\n  - SendTask(agent_id, task_json) → task_id\n  - GetPendingTasks(agent_id) → tasks_json\n  - CompleteTask(task_id, result_json) → bool\n\n## State Plugins → Tools (42)\n\nEach plugin generates 3 tools: `_query`, `_diff`, `_apply`\n\n| Plugin | Tools Generated |\n|--------|----------------|\n| systemd | plugin_systemd_{query,diff,apply} |\n| net | plugin_net_{query,diff,apply} |\n| packagekit | plugin_packagekit_{query,diff,apply} |\n| login1 | plugin_login1_{query,diff,apply} |\n| keyring | plugin_keyring_{query,diff,apply} |\n| lxc | plugin_lxc_{query,diff,apply} |\n| openflow | plugin_openflow_{query,diff,apply} |\n| systemd_networkd | plugin_systemd_networkd_{query,diff,apply} |\n| dnsresolver | plugin_dnsresolver_{query,diff,apply} |\n| netmaker | plugin_netmaker_{query,diff,apply} |\n| pcidecl | plugin_pcidecl_{query,diff,apply} |\n| privacy_router | plugin_privacy_router_{query,diff,apply} |\n| privacy | plugin_privacy_{query,diff,apply} |\n| sessdecl | plugin_sessdecl_{query,diff,apply} |\n\n## Built-in MCP Tools (28)\n\n### D-Bus Introspection (12)\n- dbus_list_services\n- dbus_introspect_service\n- dbus_list_objects\n- dbus_introspect_object\n- dbus_list_interfaces\n- dbus_list_methods\n- dbus_list_properties\n- dbus_list_signals\n- dbus_call_method\n- dbus_get_property\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3f9e-eaf8-77a0-9b28-734fd722574c"}}}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-08T02:54:40.857Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_O0bCaKSPWXCYDmIGQLhTgj5H","output":"Chunk ID: e70411\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 485\nOutput:\n//! Plugin state client — routes reads/writes through the gRPC MutationEngine\n//! (the single write door) instead of the excised D-Bus StateManager.\n//!\n//! Reads go to `RemoteOperationClient::get_state` (state_cache, the mutation\n//! fold). Writes go to `RemoteOperationClient::set_state` (ApplyPatch through\n//! the MutationEngine → EventChain → shm projection). No second write door,\n//! no StateManager, no drift.\n\nuse anyhow::{Context, Result};\nuse op_grpc_bridge::{GrpcClientPool, RemoteOperationClient};\nuse serde::de::DeserializeOwned;\nuse serde::Serialize;\nuse std::sync::{Arc, OnceLock};\n\nstatic GRPC_CLIENT: OnceLock<RemoteOperationClient> = OnceLock::new();\n\n/// Lazily initialize a singleton RemoteOperationClient backed by the\n/// MutationEngine's gRPC endpoint (env `OP_DBUS_GRPC_ADDR`, default\n/// `127.0.0.1:50051`).\nfn client() -> &'static RemoteOperationClient {\n    GRPC_CLIENT.get_or_init(|| {\n        let grpc_addr =\n            std::env::var(\"OP_DBUS_GRPC_ADDR\").unwrap_or_else(|_| \"127.0.0.1:50051\".to_string());\n        let pool = Arc::new(GrpcClientPool::new());\n        RemoteOperationClient::new(pool, &grpc_addr, \"op-web\")\n    })\n}\n\npub async fn query_plugin_state<T>(plugin_id: &str) -> Result<Option<T>>\nwhere\n    T: DeserializeOwned,\n{\n    match client().get_state(plugin_id, \"\").await {\n        Ok(state) => match simd_json::serde::from_owned_value::<T>(state) {\n            Ok(value) => Ok(Some(value)),\n            Err(_) => Ok(None),\n        },\n        Err(_) => Ok(None),\n    }\n}\n\npub async fn apply_plugin_state<T>(plugin_id: &str, value: &T) -> Result<()>\nwhere\n    T: Serialize,\n{\n    let state = simd_json::serde::to_owned_value(value)\n        .with_context(|| format!(\"serialize {} plugin state\", plugin_id))?;\n    client()\n        .set_state(plugin_id, \"\", state, \"op-web\", \"\")\n        .await\n        .map_err(|e| anyhow::anyhow!(\"apply {} state via gRPC: {}\", plugin_id, e))?;\n    Ok(())\n}\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3f9e-eaf8-77a0-9b28-734fd722574c"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-08T02:55:50.200Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. The internal path is not the DNS resolver. It is:\n\n- user signup creates a WireGuard keypair\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs` derives a route ID from the WG public key plus `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET`\n- that route object carries `selector_ip`, `ingress_port`, `next_hop`, and `container_name`\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs` turns those routes into OpenFlow rules on `ovsbr0`\n- `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs` expects the privacy chain ports `gbr_wg -> gbr_warp -> gbr_xray`\n- `deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run`, `deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run`, and `deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run` are the live service legs for that chain\n\nWhat I found on the host is that the policy is not currently materialized: `ovs-ofctl dump-flows ovsbr0` shows only the default `NORMAL` flow, and `/var/lib/op-dbus/privacy-routes.json` is not present. So the problem is not DNS resolution on the box; it is that the privacy route/OpenFlow state is not being published or applied.\n\nTo get it working, the shortest path is:\n\n- make sure `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET` is set\n- make sure the route publish path actually runs\n- make sure the OpenFlow backend is up and reachable\n- verify the chain ports exist as `gbr_wg`, `gbr_warp`, and `gbr_xray`\n- republish the privacy routes so the OpenFlow rules land on `ovsbr0`\n\nThe DNS side is only the front door. The real handoff to the right container happens in the privacy route plus OpenFlow layer, not in `/etc/resolv.conf` or the Cloudflare record script.\n\nReferences:\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs)\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs)\n- [crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run)\n\n","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":{"entries":[{"path":"MEMORY.md","lineStart":321,"lineEnd":347,"note":"oracle wireguard decoy and ingress topology context"}],"rolloutIds":[]}}}

The internal path is not the DNS resolver. It is:\n\n- user signup creates a WireGuard keypair\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs` derives a route ID from the WG public key plus `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET`\n- that route object carries `selector_ip`, `ingress_port`, `next_hop`, and `container_name`\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs` turns those routes into OpenFlow rules on `ovsbr0`\n- `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs` expects the privacy chain ports `gbr_wg -> gbr_warp -> gbr_xray`\n- `deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run`, `deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run`, and `deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run` are the live service legs for that chain\n\nWhat I found on the host is that the policy is not currently materialized: `ovs-ofctl dump-flows ovsbr0` shows only the default `NORMAL` flow, and `/var/lib/op-dbus/privacy-routes.json` is not present. So the problem is not DNS resolution on the box; it is that the privacy route/OpenFlow state is not being published or applied.\n\nTo get it working, the shortest path is:\n\n- make sure `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET` is set\n- make sure the route publish path actually runs\n- make sure the OpenFlow backend is up and reachable\n- verify the chain ports exist as `gbr_wg`, `gbr_warp`, and `gbr_xray`\n- republish the privacy routes so the OpenFlow rules land on `ovsbr0`\n\nThe DNS side is only the front door. The real handoff to the right container happens in the privacy route plus OpenFlow layer, not in `/etc/resolv.conf` or the Cloudflare record script.\n\nReferences:\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs)\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs)\n- [crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run)\n\n<oai-mem-citation>\n<citation_entries>\nMEMORY.md:321-347|note=[oracle wireguard decoy and ingress topology context]\n</citation_entries>\n<rollout_ids>\n</rollout_ids>\n</oai-mem-citation>"}],"phase":"final_answer","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3f9e-eaf8-77a0-9b28-734fd722574c"}}}

It is:\n\n- user signup creates a WireGuard keypair\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs` derives a route ID from the WG public key plus `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET`\n- that route object carries `selector_ip`, `ingress_port`, `next_hop`, and `container_name`\n- `crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs` turns those routes into OpenFlow rules on `ovsbr0`\n- `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs` expects the privacy chain ports `gbr_wg -> gbr_warp -> gbr_xray`\n- `deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run`, `deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run`, and `deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run` are the live service legs for that chain\n\nWhat I found on the host is that the policy is not currently materialized: `ovs-ofctl dump-flows ovsbr0` shows only the default `NORMAL` flow, and `/var/lib/op-dbus/privacy-routes.json` is not present. So the problem is not DNS resolution on the box; it is that the privacy route/OpenFlow state is not being published or applied.\n\nTo get it working, the shortest path is:\n\n- make sure `PRIVACY_ROUTE_SHARED_SECRET` is set\n- make sure the route publish path actually runs\n- make sure the OpenFlow backend is up and reachable\n- verify the chain ports exist as `gbr_wg`, `gbr_warp`, and `gbr_xray`\n- republish the privacy routes so the OpenFlow rules land on `ovsbr0`\n\nThe DNS side is only the front door. The real handoff to the right container happens in the privacy route plus OpenFlow layer, not in `/etc/resolv.conf` or the Cloudflare record script.\n\nReferences:\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_routes.rs)\n- [crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-web/src/privacy_openflow.rs)\n- [crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/privacy_router.rs)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-wg/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-warp/run)\n- [deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/deploy/s6/gbr-xray/run)\n\n","completed_at":1783479350,"duration_ms":541688,"time_to_first_token_ms":21953}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T17:23:17.694Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"user","content":[{"type":"input_text","text":"# AGENTS.md instructions for /home/jeremy/git\n\n<INSTRUCTIONS>\n### AGENTS.md for operation-dbus-proto\n\nThis file provides essential guidelines for agentic coding agents working in this repository. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\n\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Strict mode enabled.\n*   **Testing:** 80%+ coverage, mock externals. Name tests with behavior-focused names (`should_handle_<scenario>`).\n\n#### 7. Agent-Specific Output & Workflow Instructions\n*   **Scroll & Save Pacing:** Provide only **ONE** major component or script at a time. Wait for user confirmation before moving to the next.\n*   **Visual Cues:** If a script is a finalized component that needs to be saved to sources, it MUST begin with color bullets or icons (e.g., ⚖️ 🔴, 🟢 🛷).\n*   **Spec-Block Format:** When delivering a component, use a strict specification block containing:\n  1.  **Requirements:** The architectural rules it satisfies.\n  2.  **Design:** How it fits into the 3tched system (Zero-Copy, Btrfs, GUI Schema, etc.).\n  3.  **Code Implementation:** The exact, copy-pasteable Rust/Bash code.\n*   Before edits: `cargo check -p <crate>`, `npm run typecheck`.\n*   Mimic existing patterns: Search similar code. No new deps without PR justification.\n\n#### 8. Personal Preferences & Coding Standards\n* Refer to `~/.factory/memories.md` for personal development preferences and past decisions.\n* Follow the conventions documented in:\n  * `.factory/rules/typescript.md` - TypeScript and React conventions\n  * `.factory/rules/testing.md` - Testing and mocking standards\n\n</INSTRUCTIONS>"},{"type":"input_text","text":"<environment_context>\n  <cwd>/home/jeremy/git</cwd>\n  <shell>bash</shell>\n  <current_date>2026-07-07</current_date>\n  <timezone>America/New_York</timezone>\n  <filesystem><workspace_roots><root>/home/jeremy/git</root></workspace_roots><permission_profile type=\"disabled\"><file_system type=\"unrestricted\" /></permission_profile></filesystem>\n</environment_context>"}],"internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3d9b-047f-7e62-a290-095aa942af57"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T17:32:28.259Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"`wg-netmaker` is a real service, not just an alias. `deploy/s6/wg-netmaker/run` starts `netclient daemon`, and `deploy/s6/op-cognitive-mcp/run` defaults `WG_INTERFACE=netmaker`, so removing it cleanly would require changing that wiring first. Right now it is also `down (not started yet)`, so it is not actively running, but the config still expects it.\n\n`op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw` is not the same as `op-grpc-bridge`. The zeroclaw unit is a separate wrapper that runs `/usr/local/bin/op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw` with zeroclaw-specific bind/blob/socket env; the plain bridge runs `/usr/local/bin/op-grpc-bridge`. Same family, different service and runtime role.\n\n`op-cognitive-mcp` is down because the s6 unit is currently `down (not started yet)`, not because the latest log shows a hard crash. The latest `current` log only shows warnings, mainly missing Voyage API key / Qdrant availability / startup noise. {"timestamp":"2026-07-07T17:38:49.455Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_KCt7g04QgjD6noBf6XDFHEeV","output":"Chunk ID: 8b62c8\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 1860\nOutput:\n//! Cognitive MCP Server Binary\n//!\n//! Transports started in parallel:\n//! - HTTP/SSE  (MCP protocol, port 3003)\n//! - gRPC      (CognitiveToolService, port 50052)\n//! - D-Bus state is owned by the canonical plugin projection at\n//!   org.opdbus.v1.plugins / /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/cognitive_mcp\n//!\n//! On startup the server reads the local WireGuard public key (from the\n//! interface named by $WG_INTERFACE, defaulting to \"netmaker\") and writes the\n//! canonical IdentitySled to /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat so the Ghostbridge\n//! interceptor and Qdrant shuttle can authenticate outbound gRPC calls.\n//!\n//! Bind address resolution order (highest priority first):\n//!   1. COGNITIVE_MCP_BIND / COGNITIVE_MCP_GRPC_BIND env vars\n//!   2. --http / --grpc CLI flags\n//!   3. WireGuard interface IP detected at startup (if interface is up)\n//!   4. 0.0.0.0 fallback\n\nuse clap::Parser;\nuse op_cognitive_mcp::CognitiveMcpServer;\nuse op_identity::{write_sled_from_wg, WireGuardIdentity};\nuse tracing::{info, warn, Level};\nuse tracing_subscriber::FmtSubscriber;\n\n#[derive(Parser)]\n#[command(name = \"cognitive-mcp-server\")]\n#[command(about = \"Cognitive MCP Server with memory, NotebookLM bridge, HTTP, and gRPC\")]\nstruct Cli {\n    /// HTTP/SSE server address (MCP protocol).\n    /// If left at 0.0.0.0 the WireGuard interface IP is used when available.\n    /// Override with COGNITIVE_MCP_BIND env var or this flag.\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_BIND\", default_value = \"0.0.0.0:3003\")]\n    http: String,\n\n    /// gRPC server address (CognitiveToolService).\n    /// If left at 0.0.0.0 the WireGuard interface IP is used when available.\n    /// Override with COGNITIVE_MCP_GRPC_BIND env var or this flag.\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_GRPC_BIND\", default_value = \"0.0.0.0:50052\")]\n    grpc: String,\n\n    /// CozoDB database path\n    #[arg(\n        long,\n        env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_DB_PATH\",\n        default_value = \"/var/lib/op-cognitive-mcp/memory.db\"\n    )]\n    db: String,\n\n    /// WireGuard interface to read identity from\n    #[arg(long, env = \"WG_INTERFACE\", default_value = \"netmaker\")]\n    wg_interface: String,\n\n    /// Log level\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_LOG_LEVEL\", default_value = \"info\")]\n    log_level: String,\n\n    /// Disable gRPC server\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_GRPC_DISABLED\")]\n    no_grpc: bool,\n\n    /// Disable HTTP/SSE server\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_HTTP_DISABLED\")]\n    no_http: bool,\n\n    /// Run stdio transport only (for local MCP clients — direct, no network)\n    #[arg(long, env = \"COGNITIVE_MCP_STDIO\")]\n    stdio: bool,\n}\n\n/// Promote an `0.0.0.0:PORT` default address to `<wg_ip>:PORT` when the WG\n/// interface is up.  Explicit addresses (not starting with `0.0.0.0:`) are\n/// returned unchanged so env-var or flag overrides always win.\nfn resolve_bind(addr: &str, wg_ip: Option<&str>) -> String {\n    if let Some(rest) = addr.strip_prefix(\"0.0.0.0:\") {\n        if let Some(ip) = wg_ip {\n            return format!(\"{ip}:{rest}\");\n        }\n    }\n    addr.to_string()\n}\n\n/// Resolve bind config (http/grpc addresses, wg_interface) from the\n/// `cognitive_mcp` plugin's live `/dev/shm` projection when present. Falls\n/// back to the already-parsed CLI/env values unchanged, so a cold start\n/// (before the projection is first seeded by op-grpc-bridge) behaves exactly\n/// as it did before this wiring existed.\n///\n/// OSCAL subid: obs.service.cognitive-mcp.bind-config.resolve@v1\nfn cognitive_mcp_bind_config(\n    cli: &Cli,\n) -> op_plugins::state_plugins::cognitive_mcp::CognitiveMcpConfig {\n    use op_plugins::state_plugins::cognitive_mcp::CognitiveMcpConfig;\n\n    op_core::projection_shm::read_projection_bytes(\"cognitive_mcp\")\n        .and_then(|bytes| serde_json::from_slice::<CognitiveMcpConfig>(&bytes).ok())\n        .unwrap_or_else(|| CognitiveMcpConfig {\n            http: cli.http.clone(),\n            grpc: cli.grpc.clone(),\n            wg_interface: cli.wg_interface.clone(),\n            http_enabled: !cli.no_http,\n            grpc_enabled: !cli.no_grpc,\n            dbus_enabled: true,\n        })\n}\n\n#[tokio::main]\nasync fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {\n    let cli = Cli::parse();\n\n    let level = match cli.log_level.as_str() {\n        \"trace\" => Level::TRACE,\n        \"debug\" => Level::DEBUG,\n        \"warn\" => Level::WARN,\n        \"error\" => Level::ERROR,\n        _ => Level::INFO,\n    };\n\n    let subscriber = FmtSubscriber::builder()\n        .with_max_level(level)\n        .with_writer(std::io::stderr)\n        .finish();\n    tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(subscriber)?;\n\n    // Resolve bind config from the cognitive_mcp plugin's live projection when\n    // present (op-grpc-bridge seeds/updates it); falls back to the CLI/env\n    // values above, unchanged, when the projection is absent (cold start).\n    let bind_config = cognitive_mcp_bind_config(&cli);\n\n    // ── WireGuard identity ────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n    // 1. Detect local WG IP for bind address resolution.\n    // 2. Write canonical IdentitySled to /dev/shm for Ghostbridge auth.\n    let wg_id = WireGuardIdentity::with_interface(&bind_config.wg_interface);\n    let wg_ip = wg_id.get_local_ip();\n\n    match wg_id.get_local_pubkey() {\n        Ok(pubkey) => {\n            info!(\n                interface = %bind_config.wg_interface,\n                pubkey = %pubkey,\n                wg_ip = ?wg_ip,\n                \"Writing WireGuard identity sled to /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat\"\n            );\n            if let Err(e) = write_sled_from_wg(&pubkey) {\n                warn!(\n                    error = %e,\n                    \"Failed to write identity sled — gRPC Ghostbridge auth will not work\"\n                );\n            }\n        }\n        Err(e) => {\n            warn!(\n                interface = %bind_config.wg_interface,\n                error = %e,\n                \"Could not read WireGuard public key — identity sled not written; \\\n                 set WG_PUBKEY env var to override\"\n            );\n        }\n    }\n\n    // Resolve bind addresses: promote 0.0.0.0 defaults to WG interface IP.\n    let http_addr = resolve_bind(&bind_config.http, wg_ip.as_deref());\n    let grpc_addr = resolve_bind(&bind_config.grpc, wg_ip.as_deref());\n\n    info!(\n        http = %http_addr,\n        grpc = %grpc_addr,\n        db = %cli.db,\n        wg_interface = %bind_config.wg_interface,\n        \"Starting Cognitive MCP Server\"\n    );\n\n    let server = CognitiveMcpServer::new(&cli.db).await?;\n\n    if cli.stdio {\n        info!(\"Running stdio only (local MCP transport)\");\n        server.start_stdio().await?;\n        return Ok(());\n    }\n\n    match (!bind_config.grpc_enabled, !bind_config.http_enabled) {\n        (true, true) => {\n            eprintln!(\"Error: both gRPC and HTTP transports are disabled. Nothing to run.\");\n            std::process::exit(1);\n        }\n        (true, false) => {\n            info!(\"Running HTTP/SSE only\");\n            server.start_http_server(&http_addr).await?;\n        }\n        (false, true) => {\n            info!(\"Running gRPC only\");\n            server.start_grpc_server(&grpc_addr).await?;\n        }\n        (false, false) => {\n            info!(\"Running HTTP/SSE + gRPC\");\n            server.start_dual(&http_addr, &grpc_addr).await?;\n        }\n    }\n\n    Ok(())\n}\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3da8-9554-7300-83e3-7b946f9c09ce"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T18:29:42.068Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If you mean “stop Factory/web from reporting usage while still using the hosted web route,” you basically can’t. Anything sent through the web service can be logged, routed, metered, and reported server-side. Blocking that would either break the service or drift into bypassing provider accounting.\n\nIf you mean “stop accidental fallback / BYOM failure from silently reporting to Factory/OpenRouter,” do this instead:\n\n1. Stop using `model: auto`.\n2. Pin the exact BYOM/BYOK model.\n3. Disable fallback/free-model routing if the UI exposes that.\n4. Remove or disable OpenRouter/free provider entries you do not want used.\n5. Use direct provider API/local client instead of the web UI if you need hard control.\n6. For local Factory only, firewall/allowlist outbound traffic to just the intended provider domain, but expect hosted web to be uncontrollable.\n\nThe clean test is: pin Fable/BYOM exactly. {"timestamp":"2026-07-07T18:30:20.308Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If BYOM starts resolving correctly, you cannot stop Fable/provider usage reporting for calls that actually hit Fable. That reporting is how the provider bills. The way to prevent surprise billing is to make the route fail closed.\n\nDo this:\n\n1. **Disable `auto`** for any paid/BYOM route.\n2. **Remove or disable the Fable BYOM key** from Factory/web until you intentionally want to use it.\n3. **Set a hard spend limit at the Fable/provider account**, ideally `$0` or the smallest allowed cap.\n4. **Revoke the key** if you are not sure where it is configured.\n5. **Disable fallbacks** so a failed BYOM route errors instead of silently switching.\n6. **Pin only known-free models** when doing long unattended runs.\n\nThe strongest protection is provider-side: set the billing cap or revoke the API key. Local/web UI settings can prevent accidental routing, but only the provider account limit guarantees you do not get charged if something resolves unexpectedly.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T18:32:04.247Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If it is included in the plan and there is no key involved, then you likely cannot control provider reporting directly. The billing/usage decision happens inside the hosted plan/router.\n\nTo avoid surprise charges, the practical controls are:\n\n- Keep overage funds at `$0` if the plan hard-stops when depleted.\n- Leave paid/included premium models unpinned; use `auto` only if you accept router behavior.\n- If you want a hard fail, pin a specific paid model after overage is depleted and confirm it refuses.\n- For long unattended runs, pin explicitly free models or a local/BYOK route with a provider-side cap.\n- Check whether the web UI has toggles like `allow overage`, `premium fallback`, `auto upgrade`, or `use best available model`.\n\nGiven your evidence, the depleted overage pool may already be your safety rail. If Fable resolves and the plan enforces no-overage, it should stop instead of bill. The risk is if “included plan usage” is tracked separately from overage funds and continues silently until a delayed meter catches up.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-07-07T18:33:02.782Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If the service normally hard-cuts you off when funds are depleted, then your risk of surprise billing is probably low. If it is a billing/accounting bug, it may get corrected later, and you do not want to rely on it for anything critical.\n\nPractical way to keep it low-risk:\n\n1. Keep overage/top-up balance at `$0`.\n2. Do not add a payment method or replenish funds while testing.\n3. Use `model: auto` if that is what kept working.\n4. Avoid pinning paid Fable unless you want to test whether it hard-stops.\n5. Periodically check usage/billing during long runs.\n6. {"session_id":"019e7fe0-f681-7310-b6d1-77bdf96424c0","ts":1780271730,"text":"\\To deploy an Antigravity agent that returns structured, predictable JSON data (which you can pipe directly into your JsonRenderer in the React frontend), you need to define your interface using Pydantic and pass it to the agent configuration.\n\nHere are the actual objects and SDK references you need:\n\n1. The Schema Object (pydantic.BaseModel)\nDefine the exact JSON structure you want your UI to receive by creating a Pydantic BaseModel.\n\npython\n\n\nimport pydantic\nclass UiResponseSchema(pydantic.BaseModel):\n    action: str\n    metadata: dict[str, str]\n    confidence_score: float\n2. The Configuration Reference (LocalAgentConfig(response_schema=...))\nWhen initializing your agent, pass the Pydantic class to the response_schema parameter in your LocalAgentConfig. This forces the Gemini model to strictly conform its output to your JSON interface.\n\npython\n\n\nfrom google.antigravity import Agent, LocalAgentConfig\nconfig = LocalAgentConfig(\n    response_schema=UiResponseSchema, # Pass your schema here\n)\n3. The Extraction Reference (response.structured_output())\nAfter sending a prompt to the agent, do not rely on standard text parsing. Instead, use the structured_output() method. It will automatically parse the generated JSON and return it as a Python dictionary that safely matches your schema.\n\npython\n\n\nasync with Agent(config) as agent:\n    response = await agent.chat(\"Analyze the system status...\")\n    \n    # Retrieves the guaranteed JSON dictionary\n    json_data = await response.structured_output()\n    \n    # You can now send this json_data straight to your frontend over gRPC/HTTP\n    # for the <JsonRenderer data={sidebarContent} /> to consume.\n    print(json_data)\n7:54 PM"}

{"session_id":"019ea70a-28bc-72b2-bdad-f47cbd311c04","ts":1780919430,"text":"identity detaches fro wg protocol :'ve launched an exploration agent to map the codebase. I'll have a detailed breakdown ready once it completes — including the WireGuard session derivation, NextDNS header injection, gRPC forwarding logic, and how that maps to the concert/wristband/valet analogy.\n\nHere's the full breakdown of the zero-trust identity pipeline, mapped to the concert analogy throughout.\n\nThe Concert Analogy\nYou arrive at a venue. You hand your keys to the valet (WireGuard). The valet parks your car and gives you a claim ticket (session ID). At the door, you exchange the ticket for an all-access wristband (the Ghostbridge identity sled). Every backstage door checks the wristband — not your car, not your ticket — just the wristband. Your car (the WireGuard tunnel) never enters the venue.\n\nStage 1 — The Valet: WireGuard Handshake & Session ID Derivation\nFiles: crates/op-gateway/src/wireguard_auth.rs:529-633\n\nWhen a peer connects over WireGuard, the gateway derives three cryptographic artifacts:\n\nSession ID (the claim ticket)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:529-540\nlet input = format!(\"WG-SESSION-{}-{}\", peer_pubkey, Self::current_timestamp());\nlet session_ids = self.crypto_engine.generate_session_ids_batch(&[input.as_bytes()]);\n// → BLAKE2s hash → 128-bit hex string\nInput: Curve25519 peer public key + current timestamp\nAlgorithm: SIMD-accelerated BLAKE2s\nOutput: 16-byte hex session ID — the peer's claim ticket\nPSK (stable parking spot number)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:542-593\nlet salt = b\"WG-STABLE-PSK-2024\";  // fixed — no timestamp\n// Argon2 KDF over peer pubkey\nDeliberately does not rotate — rotating it would lock peers out mid-session, like changing the valet lot number while cars are still parked.\n\nSession Key (per-visit ephemeral)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:595-633\nlet server_nonce = self.generate_server_nonce().await?;\n// Argon2 + nonce → ephemeral key, rotated per connection\nThe Session Record (the claim stub kept by the valet)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:200-215\npub struct WireGuardSession {\n    pub session_id: String,        // BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp)\n    pub peer_pubkey: String,\n    pub psk: String,               // stable Argon2\n    pub expires_at: u64,           // 1 hour TTL\n    pub auth_method: String,       // \"wireguard\"\n    pub key_rotation_count: u32,\n    // ...\n}\nPersisted to SQLite (wireguard_sessions table) and cached in DashMap (no SQL in the hot path).\n\nStage 2 — The Wristband Printer: IdentitySled\nFiles: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs, crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs\n\nOnce the WireGuard session is established, a 152-byte shared-memory struct (/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat) is stamped — the all-access wristband:\n\nIdentitySled layout (repr(C), 152 bytes):\n  [ 0.. 32]  wireguard_pubkey    — who you are\n  [32.. 40]  mutation_index      — which version of the schema you authenticated against\n  [40.. 72]  hashed_footprint    — Blake3(current schema state) — the hologram on the wristband\n  [72.. 88]  trace_id            — UUID v4 — your unique wristband serial number\n  [88.. 92]  schema_version\n  [92..152]  reserved\n  [192..208] nextdns_profile     — e.g., \"689ec7\" — your VIP section access\nThe footprint (Blake3 hash of the live schema state) is the hologram — it proves the wristband was issued by tonight's venue, not a forgery from last week's show.\n\nThe trace_id is the serial number stamped on your wrist — immutable, linked to a Qdrant vector record for full accountability.\n\nNextDNS Profile (the VIP section pass)\n# deploy/nextdns/upsert-rewrite.py\n# Profile ID: 689ec7\n# Upserts DNS rewrites: dashboard.3tched.com → 10.0.0.1\nThe NextDNS profile ID travels with the identity sled. It tells the DNS layer which routing rules apply to this peer — their section of the venue.\n\nStage 3 — The Door Scanner: xray Header Injection\nFile: deploy/incus/privacy-xray-ingress/etc/xray/config.json:47-50\n\nxray sits at the venue entrance. It reads the wristband (sled) and stamps the metadata onto every gRPC call:\n\n\"grpcSettings\": {\n  \"serviceName\": \"Ghostbridge.StateSync\",\n  \"multiMode\": true,\n  \"metadata\": {\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Footprint\": \"<Blake3 footprint hex>\",\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID\":  \"<UUID v4 hex>\"\n  }\n}\nAt this point, WireGuard is dropped. The tunnel delivered the peer to the door; the tunnel itself does not go backstage. xray strips the WireGuard framing and forwards a plain gRPC call carrying only the two header stamps. The car stays in the lot.\n\nThe NextDNS profile influences DNS resolution at this layer — selector_ip routing directs packets to the correct Incus container before they ever reach the gRPC endpoint.\n\nStage 4 — The Backstage Guard: GhostbridgeInterceptor\nFile: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs:34-84\n\nEvery gRPC call hits this Tonic middleware on port 18789 before any handler sees it:\n\npub fn ghostbridge_interceptor(mut req: Request<()>) -> Result<Request<()>, Status> {\n    // 1. Wristband must be present\n    let footprint_value = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-footprint\").cloned();\n    let trace_value    = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-trace-id\").cloned();\n\n    if footprint_value.is_none() || trace_value.is_none() {\n        return Err(Status::unauthenticated(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Missing Ghostbridge Identity Sled. Connection Dropped.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 2. Zero-copy mmap read of the live sled (no DB hit, no network hop)\n    let (sled_ptr, _mmap) = op_identity::read_sled()?;\n    let sled = unsafe { &*sled_ptr };\n\n    // 3. Hologram check — footprint must match tonight's schema state exactly\n    let expected_footprint = hex::encode(sled.hashed_footprint);\n    if request_footprint != expected_footprint {\n        return Err(Status::permission_denied(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Temporal Hash Mismatch. Session footprint out of sync.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 4. Embed trace ID into gRPC extensions for downstream accountability\n    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_val);\n    Ok(req)\n}\nValidity rule: the sled is live only if hashed_footprint != [0u8;32] AND trace_id != [0u8;16]. A zero field means the wristband was never properly stamped — instant ejection.\n\nThe check is zero-copy — the sled lives in tmpfs (/dev/shm), mmap'd directly into the process. No SQL, no network, no disk. The guard glances at your wrist under UV light in milliseconds.\n\nStage 5 — Backstage: gRPC Routing to op-dbus\nFile: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:94-105\n\nOnce the interceptor passes the call, it routes to the internal gRPC service:\n\nDefault: http://10.200.0.2:50051  (op-dbus, inside the privacy network)\nSubnet assignments per peer come from schemas/plugin/privacy_routes.json:\n\n{\n  \"wireguard_public_key\": \"P8c9Kjnv4B3r6C4+...\",\n  \"assigned_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2/32\",    // WireGuard tunnel allocation\n  \"selector_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2\",       // OpenFlow packet-match label\n  \"container_name\": \"privacy-route-550e8400\"\n}\nOpenFlow matches selector_ip and routes to the correct Incus container. The WireGuard subnet (10.100.0.0/24) exists only to give each peer a unique identity label — it is never forwarded as a WireGuard packet beyond the gateway.\n\nA Linux user session (wg-{first12ofpubkey}) is created via loginctl enable-linger, giving the peer a D-Bus session and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR — the backstage room with their name on the door.\n\nComplete Flow, Annotated\n[Peer]\n  │  WireGuard UDP (Curve25519 handshake)\n  ▼\n[op-gateway / WireGuard endpoint]\n  │  BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp) → session_id        ← claim ticket issued\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, stable-salt) → PSK               ← stable parking spot\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, nonce)       → session_key        ← tonight's coat check\n  │  Write IdentitySled → /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat  ← wristband stamped\n  │\n  │  WireGuard framing DROPPED here ──────────────────← car stays with valet\n  ▼\n[xray ingress]\n  │  Reads sled: footprint + trace_id + nextdns_profile\n  │  Injects gRPC metadata headers:\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Footprint: <blake3-hex>\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID:  <uuid4-hex>\n  │  NextDNS profile → DNS rewrites applied (VIP section routing)\n  ▼\n[GhostbridgeInterceptor — port 18789]\n  │  Header present?    No  → 401 \"Connection Dropped\"\n  │  Footprint matches? No  → 403 \"Temporal Hash Mismatch\"\n  │  Zero-copy mmap sled read (tmpfs, no DB)\n  │  Inject trace_id into gRPC extensions\n  ▼\n[op-dbus gRPC — 10.200.0.2:50051]\n  │  Full access to internal services\n  │  Trace ID rides every call → Qdrant vector linkage for audit\n  ▼\n[Incus container — privacy-route-{user_id}]\n  └─ Linux user session, D-Bus activated, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alive\nWhy This Is Genuinely Zero-Trust\nZero-Trust Principle\tImplementation\nNever trust, always verify\tEvery gRPC call re-validates the live sled footprint — no cached \"logged in\" state\nVerify cryptographic state, not identity claims\tFootprint is Blake3 of current schema — a stale wristband from an old schema is invalid\nLeast privilege\tNextDNS profile scopes DNS; assigned_ip/32 scopes the subnet to exactly one peer\nFull audit trail\tTrace ID links every call to a Qdrant vector record — immutable, append-only\nNo implicit trust from network location\tBeing inside 10.100.0.0/24 grants nothing — the wristband check happens regardless\nThe WireGuard subnet is purely a cryptographic identity label — it gets the peer through the front door and into the valet system. The moment they're inside, the car (the tunnel) stays parked. Everything backstage runs on the wristband alone."}

{"session_id":"019ec028-2ddd-7580-9461-20e26ffa3a39","ts":1781344375,"text":"can you do this instead linux\nLinux has a mish mash of evolving protocols, the two which concern us today are Wayland and Pipewire.\n\nchrome: right now, chrome should just need -ozone-platform=wayland to natively run under wayland. It also needs WebRTC PipeWire support to capture the desktop.\n\nxdg-desktop-portal-wlr is a desktop-portal for wlroots based desktop environments such as Sway. Basically, a way for applications to access generic desktop functionality over a well known API. You'll want systemctl --user enable xdg-desktop-portal-wlr, this has activation conditions based on the environment.\n\nsway needs to trigger the start of xdg-desktop-portal-wlr, exec dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd WAYLAND_DISPLAY XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=sway should be enough.\n\nAnd magic."}

{"session_id":"019ed155-7436-7130-9370-d3b5fef38a84","ts":1781676364,"text":"April 13, 2026\nKiro CLI 2.0: a new look and feel, headless CI/CD pipelines, and Windows support\nBy\n\nDoug Clauson\n\nProduct Lead\n\n\nKrishna Dalal\n\nProduct Marketing\n\nIf you're a developer who lives in a terminal, you want a tool that fits your workflow and not the other way around. That's why we built Kiro CLI, an agentic terminal that just works, so you can ship quality code faster. Since launch, the response has been incredible. You told us what you loved, what needed work, and what was missing.\n\nWe listened. And today, we're shipping three big things you asked for:\n\nHeadless mode. Run Kiro CLI programmatically like within your CI/CD pipelines to ship releases faster.\n\nWindows support. Use your favorite Kiro agents, now natively in Windows.\n\nUX refresh, now fully GA. It gives you more control without the friction.\n\nAutomate deployments end-to-end with headless mode\nDevelopers need flexibility when coding. Running Kiro CLI within the terminal is easy, you run kiro-cli and you’re in. But what happens when you want to run it remotely without you being there?\n\nHeadless mode changes that. Generate an API key, drop it in as an environment variable, and Kiro CLI runs programmatically. You can pipe inputs, script outputs, and integrate Kiro directly into your CI/CD pipelines, build scripts, or any automated workflow. Get access to every tool, every agent, every capability you’d have in an interactive session now with programmatic access. Execute prompts like generating and publishing pull requests or running troubleshooting workflows without any user input locally, enabling true automation, so you can stay focused on innovating rather than continuously monitoring your deployments. See our blog post walking through a concrete example of using headless CLI.\n\nCreate and manage API keys for programmatic access to Kiro. Keys are shown only once upon creation. Name, Key, Created: another-test, [redacted], Apr 1, 2026; first-test, [redacted] Mar 18, 2026.\nWindows support: meeting you where you work\nThis one is personal. As a Windows person myself, I understand the frustration of not having native support and using workaround like WSL, but not anymore. I’m so excited that we now have a native Windows install for Kiro CLI. This opens up access to Kiro CLI.\n\nKiro CLI running on Microsoft Windows 11 Enterprise under PowerShell answering the question, what opearting system is this?\nYou can now use Kiro agents within the Windows Terminal app to build features in complex codebases, automate your workflow in seconds, and analyze errors and trace bugs with precision. Install the CLI to get started:\n\nInstall on macOS, Linux, or Windows\ncurl -fsSL https://cli.kiro.dev/install | bash\n\nUX refresh: less friction, more control\nSince launching the new TUI experimentally back in March, we’ve had so much great feedback. At that point, we didn’t have parity with the classic UX, but we wanted some early feedback and you delivered. You’ve called out what you liked, what was missing, and what else you’d like to see. Since then we’ve launched a new subagent experience and a way to monitor their progress and a new task list, an enhanced and updated version of the todo list, so you can easily keep track of what the agent is doing, and fixed multiple rough edges.\n\nLet’s see how the new subagent experience and task lists look like in action. For this example, I’m using subagents to build a snake game. Often we see subagents being used to parallelize the work while protecting the parent agent’s context.\n\nCan you build me a cool snake game using subagents to build it? - Let me build you a snake game using subagents! I'll split the work into parallel tracks for design/planning and then implementation. 1 tool approval pending from subagents\nTo monitor the subagent’s activity, use ctrl+g. You can see the entire trace for each individual subagent, while also seeing the status of all subagents. In this case, it’s running them back to back so you can see the flow designer → implementer → reviewer as a loop. Here is the designer in work.\n\nSubagent output. - Play area is the full terminal minus 2 rows (score line + bottom border) and 2 columns (left/right border). - Border drawn with curses box or manual line chars. - Snake and food coordinates are relative to the play area (offset by 1,1). - Direction input mapping: KEY_UP → (-1,0), KEY_DOWN → (1,0), KEY_LEFT → (0, -1), KEY_RIGHT → (0,1). Ignore input that\nwould reverse direction (e.g. pressing left while going right).\nAnd here is the reviewer, asking for increased permissions. The permission approval can be found in both the agent monitor, highlighted in yellow, as well as the main orchestrator screen.\n\nShell python3 -c import ast; ast parse(open('snake_game.py').read()); print('Syntax OK') shell requires approval\n• Yes, single permission\nTrust, always allow in this session\nTrust,\nallow all for this session\nNo\nAs the agent works, we see the task list getting updated in real-time as each step gets completed. In this case, I explicitly asked for it to be used, but the agent will do it on larger tasks by default.\n\nLet me build you a snake game! I'll create it as a browser-based game with HTML/CSS/JS, write tests, then review and fix any issues.\n\nadded 62 lines in C: \\Users\\dclauson \\snake-game\\game.js\n\nTasks (3)\n• 1. Build the snake game (HTML/CSS/JS)\n• 2. Write tests for the game logic\n• 3. Review the code and fix any issues found\n\nwrite requires approval\nAnd, there you have it, Kiro built a snake game using both the new subagents experience and the new task list experience. Give it a spin and see how subagents and the task lists work for you. The more complex the use case, the more valuable you’ll find the task list. It’ll quickly keep you up to date on what Kiro accomplished!\n\nGetting started\nThe CLI 2.0 and TUI is now the default experience. If something feels off, let us know with /feedback. Your feedback shaped everything above, and it'll shape what comes next. And if you ever want to switch back, just run kiro-cli --classic. Need more information? Be sure to check out our documentation and join the Kiro community on Discord to connect with other builders, share best practices, get technical support, and stay updated on the latest features."}

(Dropped `ovsdaemon/v1/ovsdb.proto` — it redefines every symbol from `ovsdaemon.proto`, treat it as a duplicate on the backend.)\n\nNew typed clients wired into `src/grpc/transport.ts`:\n- `adapters.proto` → `getAdaptersMailServiceClient`, `getNetmakerServiceClient`, `getMqServiceClient`\n- `cognitive.proto` → `getCognitiveToolServiceClient`\n- `assistant/*` → `getAssistantAgentServiceClient`, `getCronServiceClient`, `getAssistantMemoryServiceClient`, `getModelServiceClient`, `getNamespaceMemoryServiceClient`, `getSessionServiceClient`, `getSoulServiceClient`, `getTaskServiceClient`\n- `ovsdaemon/v1/*` → `getOvsdbServiceClient`, `getOvsdbStreamServiceClient`\n\nAll factories use the same binary `+proto` transport; aliased where names collide (`AdaptersMailServiceClient`, `AssistantAgentServiceClient`, `AssistantMemoryServiceClient`). {"session_id":"019f1378-5b9b-7c50-904b-e47e6e5c7d0b","ts":1782763760,"text":"are we using tonic build? Tim Van Wassenhove\nPassionate geek, interested in Technology. Proud father of two\n\nHome All posts Tags Contact\n28\nApr 2022\nNotes on using grpc with rust and tonic\nIn the Tonic examples proto files are used to generated service and client stubs with tonic_build.\n\nThe Getting started section mentions the following:\n\nFor IntelliJ IDEA users, please refer to this and enable org.rust.cargo.evaluate.build.scripts experimental feature.\n\nBut in order to have a nice development experience you need some additional tweaks.\n\nYou can find the full code here: https://github.com/timvw/arrow-flightsql-odbc\n\nBy default the stubs are generated in ./target/…/build/… Unfortunately CLion does not scan those folders and you don’t get to benefit from intellisense.\n\nAs a workaround you can generate the stubs in your ./src folder instead. You can do that by configuring the tonic_build in build.rs.\n\nWhile you are at it, you should also enable the writing of a file_descriptor_set to enable GRPC Server Reflection using tonic-reflection.\n\nbuild.rs\nuse std::env;\nuse std::path::PathBuf;\n\nfn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {\n\n    //intellij does not easily find types when not adding code to src\n    //tonic_build::compile_protos(\"proto/Flight.proto\")?;\n    //tonic_build::compile_protos(\"proto/FlightSql.proto\")?;\n\n    let original_out_dir = PathBuf::from(env::var(\"OUT_DIR\")?);\n\n    let out_dir = \"./src\";\n\n    tonic_build::configure()\n        .out_dir(out_dir)\n        .file_descriptor_set_path(original_out_dir.join(\"flight_descriptor.bin\"))\n        .compile(&[\"proto/Flight.proto\"], &[\"proto\"])?;\n\n    tonic_build::configure()\n        .out_dir(out_dir)\n        .file_descriptor_set_path(original_out_dir.join(\"flight_sql_descriptor.bin\"))\n        .compile(&[\"proto/FlightSql.proto\"], &[\"proto\"])?;\n\n    Ok(())\n}\nNow you can update your lib.rs and include the generated stubs by referring to their path in ./src instead of the include_proto! macro. Notice that I have also used the include_file_descriptor_set to enable the GRPC Server Reflection:\n\nsrc/lib.rs\n/*\npub mod arrow_flight_protocol {\n    tonic::include_proto!(\"arrow.flight.protocol\"); // The string specified here must match the proto package name\n}\n\npub mod arrow_flight_protocol_sql {\n    tonic::include_proto!(\"arrow.flight.protocol.sql\"); // The string specified here must match the proto package name\n}\n */\n\n#[path = \"arrow.flight.protocol.rs\"]\npub mod arrow_flight_protocol;\n\n#[path = \"arrow.flight.protocol.sql.rs\"]\npub mod arrow_flight_protocol_sql;\n\npub const FLIGHT_DESCRIPTOR_SET: &[u8] = tonic::include_file_descriptor_set!(\"flight_descriptor\");\npub const FLIGHT_SQL_DESCRIPTOR_SET: &[u8] = tonic::include_file_descriptor_set!(\"flight_sql_descriptor\");\nNow you can create your server and register the reflection service:\n\nsrc/bin/server.rs\nlet reflection_server = tonic_reflection::server::Builder::configure()\n    .register_encoded_file_descriptor_set(arrow_flightsql_odbc::FLIGHT_DESCRIPTOR_SET)\n    .register_encoded_file_descriptor_set(arrow_flightsql_odbc::FLIGHT_SQL_DESCRIPTOR_SET)\n    .build()?;\n\nServer::builder()\n    .add_service(FlightServiceServer::new(myserver))\n    .add_service(reflection_server)\n    .serve(addr)\n    .await?;\nWhen your server is running, you can query it:\n\ngrpcurl -vv -plaintext 'localhost:52358' list\nOutputs:\n\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService\ngrpc.reflection.v1alpha.ServerReflection\nWhen diving a little deeper, we find the following:\n\ngrpcurl -vv -plaintext 'localhost:52358' list arrow.flight.protocol.FlightService\nOutputs:\n\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.DoAction\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.DoExchange\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.DoGet\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.DoPut\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.GetFlightInfo\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.GetSchema\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.Handshake\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.ListActions\narrow.flight.protocol.FlightService.ListFlights\nHappy coding!"}
